Single-cell technologies and exosome biology have revealed previously unrecognized immune subsets and regulatory layers within the bone microenvironment. MAIN BODY: Osteoimmunology has elucidated the interplay between macrophages, T cells, B cells, NK cells, neutrophils, dendritic cells, and mast cells in bone remodeling. These cells form dynamic interaction networks-Treg-M2 feedback loops, Th17-neutrophil amplification, and B-T-osteoclast axes-that collectively determine net skeletal outcome. Immune cells regulate osteoclast and osteoblast function through TNF-α, IL-6, IL-17 A, and RANKL, with highly context-dependent effects. Immunosenescence has emerged as a key driver of age-related bone loss. The RANKL/RANK/OPG axis serves as the central signaling hub, modulated by Sema3A/Wnt/β-catenin, PI3K/Akt, JAK/STAT, and Notch. Dysregulation of these pathways underlies osteoporosis, RA, intervertebral disc degeneration, ankylosing spondylitis, and cancer bone metastasis. Clinically, denosumab and cytokine-targeted biologics (anti-TNF-α, anti-IL-6R, anti-IL-17 A) demonstrate bone-protective effects, while bispecific antibodies, CAR-Treg cells, and senolytics represent emerging strategies. CONCLUSIONS: The net skeletal effect of the immune system is determined by the balance of interacting cell types, cytokine networks, and signaling pathways. Future progress requires single-cell spatiotemporal multi-omics, cell-type-specific immunotherapies, elucidation of the gut-bone axis, and systematic evaluation of combination strategies pairing immunomodulators with anti-resorptives, anabolic agents, or senolytics.
42492739: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome, formally defined by the American Heart Association in 2023, affects approximately 90% of US adults, who meet criteria for stage 1 or higher. The rapid convergence of multiple drug classes on CKM pathways, SGLT2 inhibitors, finerenone, GLP-1 receptor agonists, ARNI, and interleukin-directed therapies, has created an urgent need for pharmacologically grounded frameworks that guide drug selection, interpret biomarker responses, and monitor target engagement across interconnected organ systems. This review proposes a three-dimensional biomarker-guided approach to precision pharmacotherapy in CKM syndrome. In the organ-specific dimension, we map key biomarkers to their corresponding drug targets and elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying drug-biomarker interactions: SGLT2 inhibitors attenuate myocardial injury through metabolic substrate shifting toward ketone body utilization and, based on preclinical evidence, NHE1 inhibition; neprilysin selectivity of sacubitril/valsartan explains the differential natriuretic peptide response; and tubuloglomerular feedback mediates the renoprotective hemodynamic effects of SGLT2 inhibitors. In the pathway-specific dimension, we identify cross-system biomarkers, such as hs-CRP, IL-6, galectin-3, GDF-15, and FGF21,which reveal shared druggable targets spanning the IL-1β/NLRP3 inflammasome axis (canakinumab, colchicine), IL-6 trans-signaling (ziltivekimab), and FGF21/β-klotho metabolic signaling. In the temporal dimension, we demonstrate how serial biomarker trajectories serve as pharmacodynamic readouts that distinguish therapeutic drug effects from disease progression, including the initial eGFR dip with SGLT2 inhibitors and natriuretic peptide changes during combination therapy. Central to this framework is the concept of "pharmacological phenotyping", using multi-biomarker panels to define drug-responsive pathophysiological states that directly inform therapeutic selection, analogous to companion diagnostics in oncology. We further present a comprehensive drug-biomarker interaction matrix with pharmacological rationale and analyze the emerging drug development pipeline, including RNA-based Lp(a) therapeutics, FGF21 analogues, galectin-3 inhibitors, and in vivo CAR-T anti-fibrotic approaches. This framework provides a practical roadmap for biomarker-guided precision pharmacotherapy in CKM syndrome.
42486091: Base editing (BE), the precise installation of single-nucleotide changes in DNA or RNA without inducing double-strand breaks, holds substantial therapeutic promise for correcting single-nucleotide variants, which constitute more than half of the known pathogenic genetic variants. Recent advances have improved base editor specificity, efficiency, and delivery, enabling clinically oriented procedures. Clinically, BE has shown early success or strong translational promise in sickle cell disease, β-thalassemia, leukemia (via CAR T and epitope engineering), hypercholesterolemia (PCSK9 and ANGPTL3), alpha-1-antitrypsin deficiency, and glycogen storage disease type Ia. Key remaining challenges include bystander editing within the activity window, residual off-target DNA and RNA editing, delivery constraints (payload size, tissue targeting, and redosing limits), immunogenicity, and the need for durable long-term safety evidence across relevant cell types and disease contexts. Continued technological refinements, careful preclinical validation, and rigorous clinical assessment will be essential to fully realize BE's transformative potential in precision medicine.
42469167: We previously reported poor long-term outcomes in patients with B-acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL) who developed hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH)-like toxicities (HLH-LT) after treatment with tisagenlecleucel. Since then, a consensus definition, immune effector cell-associated HLH-like syndrome (IEC-HS), was developed. Here, we report results from a multicenter retrospective study of children and young adults with B-ALL treated with tisagenlecleucel between 2018 and 2023, describing the incidence, diagnostic overlap, clinical phenotypes, and associated long-term outcomes of HLH-like syndromes. Of 154 tisagenlecleucel recipients, 14.9% met IEC-HS criteria, 21.4% met HLH-LT criteria, and 13% were identified as having HLH by treating institutions in the electronic health record; 10% met all definitions. Each HLH-like syndrome was associated with shortened overall survival and event-free survival, adjusting for baseline disease burden (P< .0001). Those with any HLH-like syndrome experienced 1-year cumulative incidence of nonresponse/relapse of 60% (95% confidence interval [CI], 43.1-76.9) vs 28.2% (95% CI, 20.0-36.5), P< .001, and nonrelapse mortality of 11.4% (95% CI, 0.7-22.1) vs 0% (95% CI, 0-0), P< .001, compared with those without. In those with high disease burden, patients with any HLH-like syndrome had a 1-year cumulative incidence of CD19- relapse of 65.2% (95% CI, 44.7-85.8) vs 2% (95% CI, 0-6.4) in those with no HLH-like syndrome, P< .001. Furthermore, adjusting for disease burden, any HLH-like syndrome was independently predictive of CD19- relapse with a hazard ratio of 8.10 (95% CI, 3.6-18.4), P< .001. These findings demonstrate partial definitional overlap of HLH-like syndromes and the prognostic significance of IEC-HS and identify CD19- relapse and nonrelapse mortality as key outcome drivers.
42467462: Notch mediates cell fate decisions in development and tissue homeostasis and can act as an oncogene or a tumor suppressor depending on the cell context. In my first essay for the GENETICS Perspectives series, "Notch and the Awesome Power of Genetics," I gave my perspective on developments in the field in the 20th century, from the isolation of the eponymous Notch mutations in Drosophila through the elucidation of the mechanism of signal transduction. That essay had a bildungsroman quality about it because the burgeoning of the Notch field and the increasing impact of Caenorhabditis elegans as a model organism coincided with my development as a scientist. But the "awesome power of genetics" was the guiding star of the essay because genetic approaches were largely responsible for identifying the core components of the signaling system and for deducing the novel cleavage mechanism by which Notch transduces signals. In this sequel, I offer my perspective as a geneticist on how the awesome power of genetics continued to have a starring role in the mechanistic discoveries that followed during the first quarter of the 21st century. I aim to show how genetics remains essential both in posing questions and in answering them even as the molecular events associated with activation of Notch signal transduction continue to be elucidated in exquisite structural detail.
42462933: BACKGROUND: Vascularized composite allotransplantation (VCA) offers life changing reconstructive options for patients with traumatic injuries or congenital defects, restoring function and appearance. Its success is limited by strong immune responses, and long-term immunosuppression carries significant risks. Emerging cellular therapies, particularly regulatory T cells (Tregs) offer promising strategies to mitigate rejection and reduce immunosuppression dependence. Preclinical studies in animal models suggest that Treg-based approaches may improve graft survival and potentially reduce the need for conventional immunosuppression in VCA. METHODS: An all-time literature search of Regulatory T cell therapy in Vascularized Composite Allotransplantation in animal models was performed on the following electronic databases: PubMed, EMBASE, Cochrane Library, Scopus, Web of Science, and TRIP Database until August 2025. Data was analyzed for graft survival, regulatory T cell activity, chimerism, and tolerance mechanisms. RESULTS: A total of 2182 studies were screened across six databases, of which 13 met eligibility criteria and 5 were selected focusing on Treg therapy in VCA animal models. Treg therapy consistently prolonged graft survival (>200 days), promoted chimerism, reduced inflammation, and induced donor specific tolerance. CAR-Tregs demonstrated antigen-specific tolerance, while mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) enhanced immunomodulation, particularly under hypoxic preconditioning. Other cellular therapies, including hematopoietic stem cells (HSC), also improved graft acceptance, demonstrating their potential as adjuncts or alternatives to long term immunosuppression. CONCLUSION: Cellular therapies, especially Treg based approaches such as adoptive transfer and local enrichment or induction of Tregs, consistently promote immune tolerance, suppress graft rejection, and extend allograft survival in VCA animal models. These approaches reduce the need for long term immunosuppression and create a pro-tolerogenic environment, supporting their translational potential. However, further clinical validation is required to optimize dosing, persistence and safety for application in human VCA recipients.
42456531: Leukemia comprises a group of hematologic malignancies characterized by pronounced molecular heterogeneity, cellular-state plasticity, and highly variable clinical outcomes. With the rapid development of high-throughput sequencing, single-cell and spatial omics, molecular measurable residual disease monitoring, and immune-engineering technologies, the diagnostic and therapeutic paradigm of leukemia is shifting from conventional morphology- and cytogenetics-based stratification toward dynamic precision medicine driven by multi-omics data. Using acute myeloid leukemia as the core model, this review systematically integrates evidence from genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics, and spatial omics to elucidate the coordinated roles of driver mutations, epigenetic regulation, leukemia stem cell plasticity, clonal evolution, the bone marrow niche, and the immune microenvironment in disease classification, risk assessment, therapeutic tolerance, and relapse. Key molecular events, including FLT3, NPM1, TP53, IDH1/2, KMT2A rearrangements, and menin-dependent pathways, have substantially advanced targeted therapy and risk-adapted management. However, single genetic abnormalities alone are insufficient to fully explain treatment response and long-term prognosis. By contrast, a multidimensional framework integrating dynamic MRD status, cellular-state transitions, functional drug vulnerabilities, and immune-ecological features may better identify relapse risk, optimize treatment sequencing, and guide the individualized application of CAR-T/CAR-NK therapy, epigenetic therapy, and combination immunotherapeutic strategies. Although multi-omics data integration, assay standardization, clinical accessibility, algorithmic interpretability, and prospective validation remain major challenges, single-cell and spatial omics, AI-assisted decision-making, and digital predictive models are expected to further promote the transition of precision medicine in leukemia from static classification to real-time monitoring, predictive modeling, and adaptive intervention. Overall, the central goal of precision medicine in leukemia is not simply to identify more molecular abnormalities, but to translate multidimensional biological information into a clinically verifiable, actionable, and continuously optimizable decision-making system.
42427031: In solid tumors, the efficacy of adoptive T cell therapy (ACT) is limited by a metabolically constrained tumor environment that undermines T cell persistence, fitness, and infiltration. Here, we engineered a hypoxia-activated bacterial hybrid system (MM@TMV) to address these barriers. This hybrid system integrates metabolically engineered bacteria and tumor membrane vesicles (TMVs) to achieve tumor-restricted metabolic reprogramming and immune reinforcement within hypoxic tumors. Within hypoxic tumors, D-mannose is produced in situ to support stem-like phenotypes and limit exhaustion, while TMVs facilitate both direct and APC-mediated activation of CAR-T and TCR-T cells, concurrently restraining tumor cell growth. In orthotopic, refractory, and metastatic tumor models, MM@TMV further improved T cell persistence, enhanced intratumoral infiltration, and achieved sustained tumor suppression. In a humanized patient-derived xenograft model of Claudin18.2-positive gastric tumors, MM@TMV similarly potentiated clinically relevant ACT. Biosafety tests confirmed systemic safety. Collectively, our findings establish engineered bacteria as programmable immune metabolic modulators that enable effective and safe ACT in solid tumors.
42237652: We present 5-year survival results in patients with relapsed or refractory (R/R) large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) from TRANSCEND NHL 001 (TRANSCEND), including data from the separate long-term follow-up (LTFU) study. Overall, 345 patients were leukapheresed and 270 received lisocabtagene maraleucel (liso-cel). Among 257 patients who were efficacy-evaluable, median overall survival (OS) was 27.5 months (95% confidence interval [CI], 16.2-47.3; leukapheresed set: 15.2 months; 95% CI, 11.5-23.4); estimated 5-year OS was 38% (95% CI, 32-45; leukapheresed set: 33%; 95% CI, 28-39). Median disease-specific survival (DSS; excludes deaths unrelated to disease progression) was 67.8 months (95% CI, 23.5 to not reached [NR]; leukapheresed set: 27.4 months; 95% CI, 14.4-69.7]); estimated 5-year DSS was 52% (95% CI, 45-59; leukapheresed set: 47%; 95% CI, 41-52). Among patients from TRANSCEND who were efficacy-evaluable, alive at study completion, and enrolled in the LTFU (n = 84), median OS and DSS were NR (95% CI, NR to NR); estimated 5-year OS and DSS were 78% (95% CI, 67-86) and 92% (95% CI, 84-97), respectively. Most deaths occurred ≤2 years after infusion; no new safety signals were observed with low rates of late severe infections and second primary malignancies. These data support the curative potential of liso-cel in patients with R/R LBCL. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT02631044 and NCT03435796.
42141200: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is a complex, aggressive and heterogeneous malignancy with trends rising rapidly worldwide. Tobacco use, alcohol consumption and human papillomavirus (HPV) infection are the leading risk factors associated with the occurrence of HNSCC. Standard treatments, including radiotherapy, chemotherapy, and surgical resection, are often associated with severe side effects and limited success, particularly in advanced, recurrent, or metastatic disease. Though the introduction of immune checkpoint inhibitors has reshaped the management of recurrent or metastatic disease, the clinical impact remains limited as a majority of patients do not achieve expected prognosis, attributed to a "cold" tumor microenvironment. Therefore, to enhance the clinical outcomes of HNSCC patients, it is priority to investigate more effective and well-tolerated targeted medicines. This review provides insights about the current treatment strategies, challenges associated with these traditional approaches along with shedding light on the state-of-the-art HNSCC treatment modalities such as advanced surgery, immunotherapy, epigenetics and cancer stem cell targeting, etc. Moreover, therapies involving varied sophisticated combinations of the abovementioned conventional approaches and these advanced treatment modalities have yielded better HNSCC prognosis in multiple preclinical and clinical settings. Continued multidisciplinary research targeting molecular pathways and innovative drug delivery systems hold the potential to remarkably enhance treatment efficacy while preserving patient's quality of life.
42919731: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a complex autoimmune disease that affects multiple organs. SSc is associated with the highest mortality rate among rheumatic diseases and significantly diminishes quality of life. Consequently, research efforts have focused on understanding its etiopathogenesis and on developing related targeted therapies. Over the past decade, organ-specific therapies (such as tocilizumab and nintedanib for lung fibrosis) have been introduced to manage various manifestations of SSc. However, there is a lack of approved therapies for the overall disease. Currently, many novel compounds are being further evaluated in ongoing clinical trials. This article reviews drugs currently in phase 2 and phase 3 trials and highlights the key disease mechanisms they target in SSc. Recent advances in understanding the pathogenesis of SSc have facilitated the identification of actionable molecular and cellular pathways, leading to the testing of targeted therapeutic strategies. Concurrently, increasing emphasis is being placed on patient stratification and personalised treatment approaches to optimise clinical trial design, improve treatment responsiveness, and enhance the generalisability of trial outcomes. Among emerging treatments, cellular therapies, including chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy, represent a significant innovation. This paradigm shift offers substantial potential for improving outcomes in systemic sclerosis.
42919351: Cancer remains a formidable challenge in global oncology, with conventional treatments often failing to achieve durable responses in advanced stages. Adoptive cell therapy (ACT), despite its revolutionary success in hematological malignancies, faces critical bottlenecks in solid tumors, including a hostile immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), restricted cellular trafficking, and the rapid onset of T-cell exhaustion. This review systematically explores the evolution of ACT platforms, ranging from foundational tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) to precision-engineered chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T and T-cell receptor (TCR)-T therapies. We highlight how innovative engineering strategies such as the integration of "armored" CARs, synthetic gene circuits, and CRISPR/Cas9-mediated gene editing have been employed to enhance the persistence and polyfunctionality of effector cells. Beyond T-cell-centric approaches, we examine the emerging landscape of diverse immune effector cells, including CAR-natural killer (NK) cells, and CAR-macrophages (CAR-M), which offer unique advantages in antigen recognition and safety profiles. Furthermore, we detail the synergistic potential of multimodal combination regimens, where ACT is paired with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), localized radiotherapy, or nanotechnology-based delivery systems to dismantle TME barriers and achieve systemic anti-tumor immunity. By tracing the journey of therapeutic cells from ex vivo expansion to intratumoral infiltration and cytotoxicity, this review illuminates the molecular mechanisms governing therapeutic efficacy. Finally, we discuss the current clinical trial landscape, manufacturing hurdles, and the regulatory pathways essential for transitioning these sophisticated cellular products from bench to bedside.
42918361: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-cell therapy has emerged as a revolutionary approach to treat various diseases, including cancers and non-cancer diseases. However, as a type of living drug, the therapeutic performance and persistence of CAR cells can be markedly affected by multiple factors, from in vitro manufacturing to in vivo conditions. In recent years, bioactive materials, especially hydrogel-based strategies, have emerged as powerful tools to improve ex vivo and in vivo CAR-cell therapy. In brief, engineered hydrogels might regulate CAR-cell expansion or activation states during manufacturing and as models for cell functional assessments in vitro; in vivo, hydrogels might preserve CAR cells and regulate their retention, release and tissue infiltration while reprogramming adverse disease microenvironments. Despite promising advances, the progress, limitations and future directions of this field have not been comprehensively evaluated. In this mini-review, we evaluate the framework of hydrogel-based strategies in boosting CAR-cell therapy over the past five years, from cell manufacturing to functional improvement. Together, current findings suggest that engineered hydrogels provide spatial and temporal cues to enhance CAR-cell manufacturing and therapeutic capacity. This review might provide insights into design principles for developing tailored hydrogels to improve CAR-cell therapies to treat diverse types of diseases.
42915066: Gene therapy has evolved into a cornerstone modality in modern medicine, with applications spanning antisense oligonucleotide treatments, RNA interference therapies, mRNA vaccines, in vivo CAR-T cell therapies, and CRISPR-mediated in vivo gene editing. The demands of this proliferating therapeutic approach compel the development of delivery systems that excel in achieving target specificity, repeat dosing compatibility, storage stability, and scalable manufacturability. Although viral vectors and lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have achieved clinical success, they face inherent challenges in fully meeting these evolving requirements, highlighting the need for alternatives. Nonviral gene delivery is a highly complex process that requires the delivery system to strike the proper balance between plasma and shelf stability, appropriate kinetic response for cargo release in the target biological milieu, and capacity for resorption or clearance from the body to minimize acute and/or long-term toxicity. Elastin-like polypeptides (ELPs), derived from human tropoelastin motifs, have emerged as promising scaffolds due to their tunable properties, low immunogenicity, and biodegradable nature. A growing number of laboratories are embracing the potential of ELPs to advance novel gene delivery systems toward these goals. This Account describes our laboratory's sustained contributions in the ELP field over the past decade, culminating in the layer-by-layer elastin-like polypeptide nucleic acid nanoparticle (LENN) platform, which is a modular and biomanufacturable nonviral gene delivery system. We pioneered a fast organic solvent extraction-precipitation purification for ELPs that is sequence independent, yields material with low endotoxin levels, and preserves the functionality of fusion domains. LENN assembly is achieved by the electrostatic condensation of nucleic acids using cyclodextrin-polyarginine conjugates to form the core, followed by coating with ELP shells through reversible host-guest interactions, producing nanoparticles capable of high RNA encapsulation. This Account presents a head-to-head design comparison of LENN versus LNPs, representative peptide-based vectors, and polymeric nonviral systems, illustrating the modularity of LENN that allows for independent optimization of key functional elements. Targeted LENN undergoes rapid internalization and endosomal escape in EGFR+ bladder cancer cells, enabling efficient mRNA expression and siRNA knockdown. Mechanistic studies confirm cellular entry via the clathrin-mediated uptake pathway and activation of lipid remodeling processes that facilitate cargo release. In an initial proof-of-concept study, EGF-modified LENN exhibited tumor association following intravesical administration in orthotopic bladder cancer models. These studies illustrate the modularity of the LENN design and its potential as a tunable, biocompatible platform for nucleic acid therapeutics.
42914683: T-cell-engaging bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) have rapidly expanded treatment options for relapsed or refractory multiple myeloma, B-cell lymphomas, and small-cell lung cancer. Their off-the-shelf availability, step-up dosing, repeated administration, and migration into outpatient and community settings distinguish them from autologous chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy. These same features increasingly bring patients to pulmonary and critical care teams. Patients receiving BsAbs may present with fever, hypoxemia, pulmonary infiltrates, pneumonia, cytokine release syndrome (CRS), secondary antibody deficiency, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PJP), cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection, respiratory viral disease, pulmonary edema, pulmonary embolism, malignant pulmonary involvement, or suspected drug-induced lung injury. Existing guidelines provide essential CRS grading, rechallenge, and infection-prevention recommendations but do not fully address the bedside pulmonary differential diagnosis, indications for bronchoscopy, ventilatory escalation, or intensive care unit (ICU) triage. This focused narrative review synthesizes pivotal trials, current prescribing information, consensus statements, real-world studies, and pulmonary literature. We emphasize two overlapping risk windows: early step-up dosing, in which CRS and infection must be evaluated and treated in parallel, and later or prolonged therapy, in which infection, target-specific immune deficits, and noninfectious mimics become dominant considerations. A timed approach using oxygen trajectory, computed tomography pattern, host immune deficits, microbiologic data, and selective bronchoscopy may reduce diagnostic anchoring and improve multidisciplinary care.
42913791: BACKGROUND: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR T) therapy has been linked with second primary malignancies (SPMs) in lymphoma treatment. However, real-world evidence assessing SPM risk in relation to conventional therapies remains limited. OBJECTIVE: This study compared the risk of SPM between patients receiving CAR T therapy and other systemic anticancer therapy (SACT) for diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. STUDY DESIGN: Adult patients who received either treatment as a second or later line of therapy (LoT) were identified from Komodo Health claims data (October 18, 2017-January 31, 2024). Inverse probability of treatment weighted incidence rates and cumulative incidences of SPM were estimated. The primary outcomes were any SPM, any hematologic SPM, and any solid SPM. Other specific outcomes included SPM by tumor type, covering cell of origin (B cell or T cell) for hematologic SPMs and specific types of SPM. RESULTS: The study evaluated 1079 CAR T therapy and 4582 SACT LoTs, with a median follow-up of 10.6 months (interquartile range: 4.3-24.3). Risk at 36 months was similar in the CAR T therapy group vs the SACT group for any SPM (37.2% vs 38.5%; P0-36 months = .06) and solid SPM (14.7% vs 17.2%; P0-36 months = .09) and for hematologic SPM (27.4% vs 27.3%; P0-36 months = .13). Lower risk for T-cell malignancies (2.6% vs 4.9%; P0-36 months = .01) and Hodgkin lymphoma (5.4% vs 7.7%; P0-36 months = .02), and higher risk for breast cancer (1.6% vs 0.6%; P0-36 months = .03) and myelodysplastic syndrome (7.1% vs 4.8%; P0-36 months = .05), was observed in the CAR T therapy group. CONCLUSION: This study found no evidence of an increased risk of any, solid, or hematologic SPMs overall in CAR T-treated patients in the short term.
42913488: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CART19) therapy represents a breakthrough for relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma (rrLBCL). However, suboptimal CART19 activity can lead to therapeutic failure and dismal outcomes. Through single cell RNA-sequencing of tumors at the time of progression from CART19, we show that a subset of tumor contain clonally expanded and proliferating populations of CART19 cells that acquire transcriptional features of dysfunction, suggestive of ongoing tumor cell engagement and chronic stimulation. Using an in vitro system to model this process, we show that iterative rechallenge of CART19 cells with target cells drives failure of tumor control associated with acquired transcriptomic features of T-cell dysfunction and reduced IL2 signaling. Pegenzileukin, a non-alpha IL2-receptor agonist, prevented CART19 dysfunction, improving T-cell expansion and tumor control in vitro. To test this concept in vivo, we developed a cell line model from a post-CART19 progression tumor that reproduces the response and failure kinetics observed in the originating patient. In vivo CART19 alone led to transient response followed by progression and secondary central nervous system relapse in this model, while the addition of pegenzileukin to CART19 led to the complete eradication of tumors. This provides mechanism-informed pre-clinical rationale for the use of non-alpha IL2 receptor agonists in combating T-cell exhaustion, a critical mechanism of CART19 failure.
42913427: T cell receptor-engineered T (TCR-T) cell therapy has emerged as a promising adoptive cellular therapy for solid tumors by enabling recognition of intracellular antigens presented via human leukocyte antigen (HLA) molecules. Unlike chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy, TCR-T cell therapy targets a broader antigen repertoire, including cancer-testis antigens, neoantigens, and viral antigens. Recent clinical advances, highlighted by the approval of afamitresgene autoleucel in synovial sarcoma, demonstrate meaningful antitumor activity. However, several limitations remain, including HLA restriction, antigen heterogeneity, toxicity related to on-target/off-tumor effects, and mechanisms of resistance such as antigen loss and T cell exhaustion. Advances in antigen selection, gene editing, and synthetic biology are improving both safety and efficacy. Combination strategies and next-generation engineered constructs are expected to overcome current barriers. This review summarizes the biological rationale, clinical evidence, safety considerations, and resistance mechanisms of TCR-T cell therapy in solid tumors and discusses future directions to optimize their therapeutic potential.
42913294: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered cells can converge on the same surface antigens in urothelial carcinoma (UC) yet depend on distinct biological steps. This creates a central uncertainty after ADC progression: whether failure reflects loss of membrane antigen or a downstream resistance mechanism that a CAR might bypass. We synthesize paired human tissue, molecular-imaging, ADC-resistance and UC-specific CAR-cell studies to examine whether an antigen targeted by a failed ADC remains suitable for cellular therapy. NECTIN4 after enfortumab vedotin (EV) provides the most direct evidence. Membranous expression often decreases between primary and metastatic UC, and serial observations document lesion-specific loss. However, selected post-EV biopsies and resistant models retain NECTIN4; in those models, NECTIN4 CAR T cells remain active. Transporter and payload-resistance studies further support target-independent failure. Evidence for HER2 and TROP2 is less direct but suggests that alternative antigens may remain available when NECTIN4 declines. We therefore propose a resistance-state framework: same-target CAR development requires recent evidence of accessible membrane antigen; target loss or marked heterogeneity favors target switching or multi-target strategies; and unresolved states require biomarker-rich testing. Current evidence does not support a clinical treatment sequence. Instead, it defines the sampling, biomarker and correlative-study requirements needed to make post-ADC CAR trials interpretable.
42913258: BACKGROUND: Previous studies identified CD20+ cells within the melanoma tumor microenvironment, including tumor-associated B-cells and putative cancer stem cells (CSC), as potential therapeutic targets. We therefore evaluated CD20-targeting CAR T-cells in patients with advanced melanoma. METHODS: This prospective, open-label phase I trial evaluated a 3 +3 design in patients with advanced melanoma, refractory to approved treatments, to assess safety and preliminary activity of autologous anti-CD20 CAR T-cells (MB-CART20.1). Following lymphodepleting chemotherapy, patients received a single MB-CART20.1 infusion. Primary endpoints were safety and tolerability; secondary endpoints included kinetics and early evidence for antitumor activity. Three patients received dose level 1 (DL1) (1.0 ×10⁵ cells/kg) and four patients DL2 (1.0 ×10⁶ cells/kg). RESULTS: No DLTs occurred at DL1, while two patients experienced DLTs at DL2 (grade 3 ICANS and grade 4 hepatotoxicity). Overall, 43 serious TEAEs were reported across all seven patients. Stable disease was observed in three patients at week 16; all had progressed by month 6. All had received immune checkpoint inhibitors within 6 months before leukapheresis and showed reduced exhaustion marker expression on CD8+ T-cells. In addition, the frequency of CD19+CD24+CD27+ Breg cells trended to associate with progressive disease and inversely correlate with toxicity. MB-CART20.1 showed robust in vivo expansion however, severe DLTs at DL2 without durable clinical benefit led to early trial termination. CONCLUSIONS: In advanced melanoma, MB-CART20.1 was associated with marked expansion and toxicity, suggesting that Breg depletion and the melanoma-typical treatment history might have driven distinct CAR T-associated immunotoxicities.
42913010: Liver fibrosis is a severe complication of diverse chronic liver diseases characterized by a dysregulated hepatic microenvironment, and effective clinical therapeutic strategies for this condition remain lacking to date. Chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR-Ms) hold considerable therapeutic potential for liver fibrosis via antigen-specific recognition and efferocytotic activity, yet their clinical translation is largely hindered by the sophisticated ex vivo preparation procedures. Herein, we report an in situ CAR-M engineering strategy that uses a phosphatidylserine (PS)-incorporated, macrophage-targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) for the codelivery of CAR messenger RNA (mRNA) and Cas9 mRNA in vivo. Our findings demonstrate that this engineered LNP achieves efficient targeting of liver-resident macrophages. Transfection with fibroblast activation protein α (FAPα)-CAR mRNA equips macrophages with the capacity to specifically target activated hepatic stellate cells (aHSCs), whereas Cas9-mediated follistatin-like protein 1 (FSTL-1) gene editing enhances the efferocytotic function of macrophages in liver tissues. Consequently, functional CAR-Ms are generated in situ, which elicits robust antifibrotic effects, including reduced collagen deposition, restored sinusoidal architecture and enhanced immune-mediated antifibrotic activity. Collectively, our customized LNP-mediated in situ engineering of liver macrophages into CAR-Ms enables precise antifibrotic intervention for liver fibrosis and circumvents the cumbersome ex vivo CAR-M preparation process.
42911633: Glioblastoma (GBM) harboring EGFRvIII represents a biologically distinct and highly aggressive tumor subset characterized by aberrant receptor signaling, marked intratumoral heterogeneity, and profound immune remodeling. Rather than acting as a constitutively active truncated receptor, EGFRvIII represents a structurally rewired EGFR variant whose altered extracellular architecture, receptor assembly, and trafficking promote ligand-independent signaling and signaling plasticity, thereby supporting tumor proliferation, stemness, invasion, and angiogenesis. Beyond tumor-intrinsic effects, EGFRvIII also contributes to the formation of a spatially heterogeneous, myeloid-dominant and immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, characterized by myeloid-cell expansion, impaired T cell effector function, and mesenchymal-like tumor-immune plasticity. Despite extensive therapeutic efforts including tyrosine kinase inhibitors, monoclonal antibodies, vaccines, immune checkpoint blockade, and EGFRvIII-targeted CAR-T cell strategies, durable clinical efficacy remains limited by the interplay of antigen heterogeneity, adaptive signaling, clonal evolution, and microenvironmental immunosuppression. Taken together, EGFRvIII can be viewed as a structural and evolutionary regulator that links receptor rewiring and signaling plasticity with immune ecosystem remodeling and therapeutic resistance, underscoring the need for integrated strategies that target both tumor cell-intrinsic signaling and the suppressive microenvironment.
42911173: INTRODUCTION: Fibroblast activation protein (FAP) is a membrane-bound serine protease highly expressed by activated stromal cells in the majority of epithelial-derived malignancies, on the contrary FAP expression is limited in normal adult tissues. Beyond the recognizing role as a marker of cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs), accumulating evidence indicates that FAP actively contributes to extracellular matrix remodeling, immune suppression, tumor progression and therapeutic resistance, making it an attractive target for both cancer diagnosis and treatment. AREAS COVERED: We summarize current knowledge regarding the molecular organization, enzymatic functions and regulatory mechanisms governing the expression of FAP as well as its role within the tumor microenvironment. We further discuss recent advances in FAP-directed strategies, encompassing molecular imaging and theranostics, antibody-based agents, enzyme-activated prodrugs, CAR-engineered immune cells, vaccines, nanocarriers and extracellular vesicle-based delivery systems. EXPERT OPINION: FAP has emerged as one of the most promising stromal biomarkers in precision oncology. Nevertheless, CAF heterogeneity and context-dependent biological functions. Future efforts integrating spatial multiomics, radiomics and artificial intelligence are expected to refine patient stratification and facilitate the clinical implementation of FAP-targeted theranostic and immunomodulatory approaches.
42909984: Immune checkpoint immunotherapy has transformed contemporary oncology, establishing a new paradigm across diverse malignancies. P-selectin glycoprotein ligand-1 (PSGL-1; CD162) emerged as a new immunotherapeutic target. Initially characterized as a glycosylated selectin ligand controlling leukocyte rolling, adhesion, and trafficking, PSGL-1 is now recognized as a multifunctional immunoregulatory receptor with therapeutic relevance in cancer. Its mucin-like structure, specific glycosylation, tyrosine sulfation, and cellular context enable functional interactions with several ligands, including selectins and V-domain immunoglobulin suppressor of T cell activation (VISTA). PSGL-1 is known to shape immune homeostasis, T-cell activation, effector and memory T-cell differentiation, myeloid-cell function, and tumor immune evasion. In chronic infection and cancer models, PSGL-1 restrains antigen-driven T-cell responses and contributes to dysfunctional or exhausted T-cell states, supporting its classification as a checkpoint-like regulator of immunity. Importantly, genetic deletion or antibody-mediated blockade of PSGL-1 enhances anti-tumor immunity in preclinical cancer models by increasing tumor-infiltrating T-cell activation and promoting immunostimulatory myeloid phenotypes. These changes in tumor-infiltrating immune cells are associated with reduction of tumor growth, synergism with PD-1/PD-L1 blockade, and improvement of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy. In blood cancers, where PSGL-1 is often expressed in malignant cells, PSGL-1 contributes to malignant cell homing, tissue dissemination, chemoresistance, and antibody-induced tumor-cell apoptosis. Overall, PSGL-1 represents a promising candidate for next-generation cancer immunotherapy, with potential to stimulate anti-tumor immunity, remodel the tumor microenvironment, and target malignant hematopoietic cell properties.
42909844: INTRODUCTION: This study evaluated the cost-effectiveness of lisocabtagene maraleucel (liso-cel) versus axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) as a second-line treatment for patients with primary refractory or early relapsed transplant-eligible large B cell lymphoma (LBCL) from a US commercial third-party payer perspective. METHODS: A partitioned survival model captured the event-free, post-event, and death states to estimate incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) from cost and quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs) over a lifetime horizon. Mixture cure modeling was employed to extrapolate event-free survival (EFS) and overall survival (OS) beyond the trial follow-up period using data from the TRANSFORM and ZUMA-7 studies. The comparative treatment effect of liso-cel versus axi-cel was estimated using the Bucher method for indirect treatment comparisons, leveraging standard of care as a common comparator across both trials. Health state utility estimates and disutilities due to adverse events (AE) were derived from TRANSFORM EQ-5D-5L data and supplemented with published sources. The model incorporated costs associated with chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy pre-treatment, treatment acquisition and administration (inpatient and outpatient), subsequent treatment, AE management, hospitalization after infusion, monitoring, and end-of-life care based on standard US sources. RESULTS: Liso-cel was projected to result in additional QALYs of 0.31, at a lower cost than axi-cel (incremental cost of - $9398). The cost of liso-cel was offset by lower costs associated with AE management (- $11,109), chimeric antigen receptor T cell administration (- $15,074), and subsequent treatment (- $2864). The main driver of results was the OS cure probability. CONCLUSION: Liso-cel as a second-line LBCL treatment was estimated to be cost-effective compared with axi-cel, as informed by pivotal trials, from a US commercial third-party payer perspective. Patients treated with liso-cel were estimated to gain slightly more QALYs at a lower cost. TRIAL REGISTRATION: NCT03575351 (TRANSFORM), NCT03391466 (ZUMA-7).
42909255: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematological malignancies, yet its efficacy in solid tumors remains limited by inefficient trafficking, suppressive myeloid and regulatory T-cell populations, and metabolic stress. These barriers contribute to incomplete tumor cell killing and loss of CAR-T cell function. Chemokines are usually viewed as migratory guides, but in solid tumors they also orchestrate immune cell positioning and inflammatory state. In this review, we discuss how chemokine gradients form inflammatory niches and control CAR-T-cell recruitment, intratumoral distribution, retention, and egress. We also examine how chemokine programs interact with cytokine signaling and regulated tumor cell death to shape local and potentially tissue-wide antitumor immunity, including through the release of damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). Finally, we outline translational strategies that include engineered chemokines and matched chemokine receptor programs to enhance the efficacy of chemokine/cytokine-armored CAR-T cells, and related combination therapies.
42909156: Neuroblastoma (NB) is one of the most challenging paediatric malignancies, accounting for 15% of childhood cancer-related deaths. It is characterised by a high heterogeneity ranging from spontaneous regression to high frequency of metastatic disease at diagnosis. Although current treatment strategies, including chemotherapy, surgery and radiotherapy, have improved outcomes, recurrence often occurs in high-risk NB patients, thus affecting overall survival. In this context, personalised medicine is emerging as a promising approach taking advantage of predictive biomarkers to refine risk stratification and to predict treatment response, together with the development of innovative treatments for high-risk NB. This review summarises the landscape of biomarkers in NB, focusing on genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and metabolomic signatures associated with aggressive disease biology, therapeutic resistance, and clinical outcome. We highlight how improved patient stratification could help to identify actionable targets resulting in innovative therapeutic strategies. These include GD2-directed immunotherapy, CAR-T and CAR-NK cell approaches, and pathway-directed agents targeting mainly ALK, and MYCN-associated dependencies. Ultimately, the transition from standardised protocols to a systematic integration of multidimensional biomarker profiles with next-generation therapies promises to transform the clinical management of high-risk NB. Addressing the biological complexity of NB ensures more effective and less toxic interventions, paving the way for personalised therapeutic approaches aimed at preventing relapse in high-risk cases and significantly improving long-term survival.
42909135: INTRODUCTION: Cell expansion is one of the most critical steps in the development of CAR-T cell manufacturing processes because it directly influences cell yield and process performance. The systematic optimization of expansion parameters using primary human T cells is often limited by inter-donor variability, cost, and experimental complexity. So, it is necessary to study more homogeneous populations that allow to stablish standardized conditions in a controlled environment that were able to be used as standard. So, in this study, we developed a Jurkat CAR-CD19 cell-based platform as a reproducible model for optimizing the cell expansion bioprocess under controlled culture conditions. METHODS: CAR-CD19-expressing Jurkat cells were pre-generated, molecularly characterized and subsequently used to evaluate key bioprocess variables, including glucose concentration, inoculum density, culture medium composition (RPMI + 10% FBS versus Nutri-T without serum), shaking speed, and different culture operating modes (batch, fed-batch, and semi-perfusion). Cell growth kinetics, metabolite consumption, metabolite production, and CAR expression were evaluated throughout the optimization process. RESULTS: An intermediate glucose concentration supported cell expansion without additional benefit from higher glucose supplementation. Serum-free Nutri-T medium promoted higher viable cell densities than RPMI (used as control media) under the evaluated conditions. Among the operating modes evaluated, semi-perfusion achieved the highest viable cell density, maintaining high cell viability and a homogeneous CAR-positive cell population at the end of culture in Nutri-T media. CONCLUSION: These findings demonstrate that the Jurkat CAR-CD19 model provides a robust and reproducible experimental platform for optimizing cell expansion bioprocesses. While further validation in primary human CAR-T cells is required, this model allows for the systematic evaluation of culture variables, minimizing experimental variability and facilitating early-stage process development for adoptive cell therapies.
42908664: OBJECTIVE: Although several CAR-T products have been approved for hematologic malignancies, their post-marketing adverse-event reporting patterns may not be interchangeable. This study compared FAERS-derived positive signals across approved CAR-T products to distinguish recurrent class-related toxicities from product-skewed reporting patterns. METHODS: FAERS reports from Q1 2014 to Q2 2025 were reviewed for CAR-T products. Demographic characteristics were summarized for seven products, whereas PT- and SOC-level signal analyses were restricted to six products with sufficient signal data: Breyanzi, Kymriah, Tecartus, Yescarta, Abecma, and Carvykti. Positive signals were detected using ROR, PRR, and BCPNN algorithms. After predefined exclusion of nonclinical or non-AE terms, indication- or disease-progression-related terms, procedure- or investigation-related terms, efficacy- or persistence-related terms, and product-quality-related terms, eligible signals were compared at the PT and SOC levels. Nonspecific MedDRA-coded PTs were retained if they met the predefined signal criteria, but they were interpreted descriptively and were not used to define product-level profile labels. RESULTS: CRS was consistently among the leading PT-level signals across all six products. Yescarta and Tecartus showed higher reporting of ICANS and neurotoxicity-related PTs. Kymriah was more strongly represented by infection-, immune-, and hematologic-related signals, whereas Carvykti showed several neurologic PTs including Parkinsonism, cranial nerve paralysis, facial paralysis, and Bell's palsy. Abecma showed relatively high-ranking systemic symptom-related PTs, including fatigue, headache, and decreased appetite. At the SOC level, nervous system disorders and infections and infestations were among the most frequently represented categories, but their proportions differed across products. CONCLUSION: FAERS-based signal detection showed a common CAR-T reporting backbone centered on CRS, ICANS/neurotoxicity, hypotension, pyrexia, infection-related events, and hematologic events, together with product-skewed signal patterns. These findings represent disproportionality signals rather than comparative safety rankings, and FAERS data cannot establish causal relationships between CAR-T products and adverse events.
42907869: Breast cancer develops within spatially organized, multicellular microenvironments in which particular tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) states can influence immune access and stromal remodeling. Conventional M1/M2 classification and total macrophage density fail to capture the developmental, transcriptional, metabolic, and spatial heterogeneity that determines TAM function. This macrophage-focused review examines breast cancer within its multicellular microenvironment, integrating lineage-tracing, single-cell, spatial, mechanistic, and clinical evidence while distinguishing breast-specific findings from hypotheses extrapolated from other tumors. We examine how tissue-resident and monocyte-derived macrophages are recruited, retained, expanded, and reprogrammed across primary and metastatic sites, emphasizing interactions with malignant cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts, extracellular matrix, vasculature, adipose tissue, and lymphoid populations. In defined breast-tumor contexts, TAM programs have been implicated in immune exclusion, invasion, metastatic dissemination, and adaptation to systemic treatment, although evidence strength varies across mechanisms and therapeutic modalities. Small and heterogeneous clinical studies have not established a benefit from broad CSF1/CSF1R-axis targeting in breast cancer, despite encouraging preclinical findings. Accordingly, we highlight a shift toward state-selective, spatially resolved, and temporally coordinated targeting. Emerging approaches include restoring phagocytosis, disrupting chemokine and fibrotic circuits, metabolic reprogramming, and converting suppressive TAMs into inflammatory, antigen-presenting effectors. A major focus is chimeric antigen receptor macrophage (CAR-M) therapy, which combines antigen-directed phagocytosis with tumor infiltration, matrix remodeling, antigen presentation, and recruitment of endogenous immunity. Although early clinical data support manufacturing feasibility, tumor trafficking, and acceptable initial safety, limited antitumor activity underscores challenges involving antigen heterogeneity, persistence, metabolic fitness, biodistribution, and scalable production. We propose a translational roadmap integrating spatial biomarkers, quantitative target selection, macrophage-adapted CAR design, checkpoint-resistant phagocytosis, metabolic engineering, safety switches, and biomarker-guided combination therapy. This framework positions macrophage reprogramming as a context-dependent strategy for modifying selected breast-tumor niches, with therapeutic targets chosen according to the macrophage program and its surrounding cellular architecture.
42907595: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells have revolutionized the treatment of B-cell malignancies but have not yet succeeded in acute myeloid leukemia (AML), largely due to the lack of cell surface antigens that can distinguish leukemia cells from essential normal hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs). Here, we used a newly developed high-affinity monoclonal antibody (mAb) B16, which is specific for the surface ROR2 in both human and mouse. Although ROR2 is a developmentally restricted protein that is primarily expressed during embryogenesis, we find that ROR2 protein is generally expressed by AML cells, including leukemia stem cells (LSCs), in patients with adverse-risk disease. Consistently, ROR2 is undetectable in most normal postnatal tissues and HSCs. Additionally, ROR2 can activate STAT3 signaling in response to Wnt11 in AML. Employing the binding domain of the anti-ROR2 mAb, we generated anti-ROR2 CAR T cells that selectively eliminated ROR2-positive AML cells of these patients while sparing normal HSCs. Intravenous infusion of such anti-ROR2 CAR T cells into immune-deficient mice selectively eradicated engrafted ROR2-positive human AML cells, including LSCs, without adversely affecting non-neoplastic normal mouse tissues or hematopoiesis. We propose that anti-ROR2 CAR T cells may offer therapeutic benefit for AML patients.
42907426: Epigenetic reprogramming underlies innate immune memory. However, whether trained immunity can be induced via epigenetic intervention to combat tumors, and the key regulators controlling this process, remain unclear. Here, we demonstrate that histone deacetylase inhibitor (HDACi) priming establishes a trained immunity-like state in monocytes/macrophages, conferring potent antitumor effect in multiple models of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) in female mice. Interferon regulatory factor 8 (IRF8) is identified as the master regulator of the inflammatory transcriptional program, which is governed by IRF8-associated super-enhancers and reinforced by HDACi. Myeloid-specific IRF8 deficiency impairs pro-inflammatory macrophage differentiation and abrogates HDACi-induced antitumor efficacy. Moreover, an IRF8-driven, CCL8-expressing macrophage subset recruits and activates cytotoxic CCR5+CD8+ T cells in the TNBC microenvironment. As a proof-of-principle with translational relevance, CCL8-overexpressing EGFR-targeted CAR T cells exhibit enhanced trafficking and improved efficacy in a humanized TNBC model. Our study defines the IRF8-CCL8-CCR5 axis as an epigenetically potentiated nexus of innate and adaptive antitumor immunity.
42907136: Despite innovative progress, cellular therapies have not produced durable, population-level survival gains in glioblastoma. Across 3 major modalities, engineered effectors such as chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) and natural killer (NK) cells, immune-education platforms such as dendritic and whole-cell vaccines, and carrier cells delivering oncolytic or drug payloads, trials have shown measurable bioactivity, but durability has varied. This likely reflects systemic barriers, including therapy-induced lymphopenia, myeloid dominance, and T-cell sequestration, as well as local barriers such as antigen heterogeneity and immune suppression. To understand why some studies nevertheless showed more favorable efficacy signals, we reviewed clinical outcomes across these modalities and identified 4 recurring design features that appeared repeatedly among studies reporting more favorable survival signals: treatment in the minimal residual disease setting, a T-helper type 1 supportive context, broadened antigenic coverage, and effective immune hand-off from the initiating therapy to endogenous or adoptively transferred effectors. Across heterogeneous early-phase studies, greater feature alignment sometimes co-occurred with more favorable signals, although this retrospective pattern is descriptive and does not establish association or causality. These observations may help guide future biomarker-informed strategies and provide a practical framework for organizing multimodal trials aimed at converting transient bioactivity into more durable, polyclonal control.
42906902: The CAR-HEMATOTOX model has been shown to help identify patients with relapsed/refractory (R/R) large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL) at heightened risk of severe neutropenia, serious infection and worse clinical outcomes after chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. We evaluated whether CAR-HEMATOTOX scores had prognostic value in patients with R/R follicular lymphoma (FL) or diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) treated with odronextamab (cluster of differentiation [CD]20 × CD3 bispecific antibody) in the ELM-1 (NCT02290951) and ELM-2 (NCT03888105) studies. Patients were retrospectively stratified by baseline CAR-HEMATOTOX score: CAR-HEMATOTOX score low (HTlow [0-1]; FL, n = 115, DLBCL, n = 92) or CAR-HEMATOTOX score high (HThigh [≥2]; FL, n = 24, DLBCL, n = 98). The incidence of grade ≥2 cytokine release syndrome within the first 30 treatment days, and rates of grade ≥3 infection and delayed neutrophil recovery within the first 90 treatment days, were numerically higher in HThigh versus HTlow patients. In patients with HThigh versus HTlow scores, progression-free survival (PFS) was significantly poorer in DLBCL (2.6 vs. 9.6 months [p < 0.0001]), and overall survival (OS) was significantly worse in FL and DLBCL (FL, 26.5 months vs. not reached [p = 0.030]; DLBCL, 4.8 vs. 17.2 months [p < 0.0001]). These results suggest that the CAR-HEMATOTOX score may provide a readily available measure for identifying patients at risk of inferior clinical outcomes with odronextamab treatment.
42906792: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has revolutionized the treatment for patients with aggressive relapsed or refractory B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (B-NHL). One notable complication is immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) which can be life-threatening. Treatment includes supportive care along with corticosteroids, often for protracted time periods. While ICANS presentation can be variable, it was previously unknown whether patients experiencing ICANS and treated with steroids had reduced CAR-T cell activity and worse outcomes. In addition, the optimal predictors of severe ICANS prior to lymphodepletion remain incompletely understood with a few studies suggesting utility of the endothelial stress activation index (EASIX) score or the modified EASIX score (m-EASIX). We conducted a multicenter retrospective analysis of 352 patients who received axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) or tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel) for the treatment of B-NHL. In this cohort 125 patients developed ICANS (35.5%). Survival was not different among patients who did not develop ICANS, with median PFS of 4.1 months (vs 9.5 months in those who developed ICANS, P = 0.37) and median OS in patients who did not develop ICANS was 25.3 (vs 15.2 months in those who developed ICANS, P = 0.16). Evaluation of the EASIX and m-EASIX scores in our data set demonstrated limited discriminatory ability in predicting development of ICANS (AUC 0.64 and 0.66 respectively). Additionally, CRP alone performed similarly to these scores (AUC 0.64), highlighting the need for novel predictive models for severe ICANS which might aid in appropriate product selection and lead to strategies to prevent neurologic toxicity after CAR-T treatment.
42906542: Efficient integration of gene-length cargos in vivo remains challenging. Non-long terminal repeat (non-LTR) retrotransposons, which naturally mobilize large DNA segments through an RNA intermediate, could potentially address these limitations. Here, we developed a computational pipeline to systematically identify a diverse set of non-LTR retrotransposons. Extensive engineering generated elements capable of the efficient and stable insertion of reporter genes in human cells using RNA templates introduced in trans, which we term Gene Writers. Gene Writers successfully generated CD19 and CD20 chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells ex vivo with robust antitumor activity. Lipid nanoparticle-mediated RNA delivery enabled in vivo CAR-T cell generation and stable B cell depletion in a humanized mouse model. Our study delineates a comprehensive framework for the discovery, engineering, and application of non-LTR retrotransposons and demonstrates their utility for gene-sized cargo delivery in vivo, thereby bridging a critical gap in existing gene therapy modalities.
42906538: T cell exhaustion limits the success of cancer immunotherapies, yet the proteomic changes underlying this dysfunctional state remain poorly understood. We integrated transcriptomics, quantitative proteomics, turnover proteomics, and ubiquitin proteomics to construct a multi-omic atlas of T cell exhaustion. These studies identified pathways regulated through transcriptional and post-translational mechanisms, including degradative and nondegradative ubiquitin modifications, and uncovered widespread changes in proteostasis, metabolism, and DNA repair. Major shifts were revealed in the ubiquitin-proteasome system, as differential expression of E3 ubiquitin ligases correlates with immunotherapy outcomes. These findings position the collapse of proteostasis as a central, underappreciated feature of T cell exhaustion and reveal opportunities to restore T cell function. We demonstrate that overexpression of the E3 ligase RNF166 enhances T cell persistence in vitro and in vivo. This work defines proteome-turnover dynamics as a critical regulatory layer in progressive T cell dysfunction, with broad implications for advancing cancer immunotherapy through manipulation of E3 ligases.
42906410: INTRODUCTION: Anti-CD19 CAR T-cell therapy has improved outcomes in B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma (B-NHL), but only about half of patients achieve durable benefit. As CD20 is expressed in > 90% of B-NHL, this phase I trial evaluated the CD20-directed CAR T-cell product MB-CART20.1 in adults with relapsed/refractory CD20-positive B-NHL without curative treatment options. METHODS: In this phase I dose-escalation trial, patients received 1.0 × 10⁵ cells/kg body weight (BW) MB-CART20.1 at the safety dose level (SDL) or 1.0 × 10⁶ cells/kg BW at dose level 1 (DL1). RESULTS: Recruitment was terminated early because of the COVID-19 pandemic after nine heavily pretreated patients had received MB-CART20.1 (SDL n = 7; DL1 n = 2). Diagnoses included transformed follicular lymphoma (n = 4), diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (n = 3), Richter transformation from chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL, n = 1), and small lymphocytic lymphoma (n = 1). One dose-limiting toxicity (DLT; grade 4 neutropenia) occurred at DL1; the maximum tolerated dose was not determined. No grade ≥ 3 cytokine release syndrome occurred (grade 1: n = 4; grade 2: n = 1). One patient developed grade 2 immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome. The best overall response rate was 56%, including 33% complete responses (CR; SDL n = 1; DL1 n = 2). CRs were durable, with one maintained through 5 years of follow-up. CAR T-cells showed robust expansion, with higher Cmax at DL1 than SDL (125.9 vs. 3.1 cells/µL). Cmax and AUC0-28D were higher in responders (p = 0.0369). CONCLUSION: With manageable toxicity, no DLTs at SDL, and preliminary signs of efficacy in the overall trial cohort, these findings warrant further investigation of CD20-directed CAR T-cell therapy in relapsed/refractory B-NHL.
42905561: T cell activation relies on the coordinated integration of T cell receptor (TCR) and cosignaling pathways, yet how these signals are physically organized remains unclear. Here, we demonstrate that CD28 co-stimulation is driven by a condensation mechanism in which the CD28 intracellular domain (ICD) forms signaling condensates with the Src-family kinase Lck. Ligand engagement promotes CD28 ICD accessibility and triggers rapid CD28/Lck condensation, enhancing CD28 phosphorylation, cytoskeletal polarization, and cytokine production. The downstream effectors of CD28, including PI3K and GRB2, can also be recruited into the CD28-Lck condensates in our reconstituted system. We further identify PD-1 as a graded regulator of this process: Monophosphorylated PD-1 is recruited into CD28/Lck condensates, whereas diphosphorylated PD-1 competitively binds the CD28 ICD and dissolves these assemblies. CD28 and PD-1 ICDs also undergo condensation directly, revealing a dynamic and compositionally heterogeneous signaling system. Guided by this competitive condensation mechanism, we engineer CD28 ICD mutants that preserve Lck condensation while resisting PD-1-mediated disruption. Incorporation of these condensation-selective mutants into Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) constructs confers resistance to inhibitory signaling and enhances antitumor efficacy in vivo. These findings establish condensation as a central organizing principle of CD28 costimulation and provide a biophysical framework for engineering more resilient therapeutic T cells.
42905522: Engineered T and NK cell therapies have widely been used to treat hematologic malignancies and solid tumors, with promising clinical results. Current chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapeutics are, however, associated with treatment-related adverse events such as cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and are prone to immunologic exhaustion. CAR-NK therapeutics, while not associated with CRS, have limited in vivo persistence. We now demonstrate that a population of NK-like TCRαβ+ CD8 T cells (TKLR), identified and expanded ex vivo through its expression of the activating receptor NKG2C, can be transduced to express a second-generation CD19 CAR (1928z). These CAR+ TKLR demonstrates superior tumor clearance and longer persistence compared to 1928z CAR+ conventional CD8 T cells (TConv) and 1928z CAR+ NK cells in mouse xenograft models. Moreover, CAR-modified TKLR had decreased expression of PD-1, TIM-3, and LAG-3 and elicited significantly reduced CRS compared to CAR+ CD8 TConv in mouse xenograft models. Similarly, NKG2C+ TKLR engineered with a TCR targeting the NY-ESO-1 antigen exhibited robust tumor control compared to TCR-engineered CD8 TConv in a mouse xenograft model. These data establish NKG2C+ TKLR as a promising platform for cell engineering, and offer a safer, more durable alternative to conventional CAR-T and CAR-NK therapies.
42905219: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This review evaluates the evolving landscape of cardiovascular toxicities associated with two pillars of modern cancer treatment: immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. It examines their distinct immune-mediated pathophysiologies, clinical manifestations, and management frameworks. RECENT FINDINGS: While ICIs carry a clinical trial incidence for cardiotoxicity of approximately 1%, real-world data suggest rates of 3-5%, with myocarditis sometimes manifesting early as part of a high-mortality "Triple M" or overlap syndrome. Major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) occur in nearly 50% of ICI-myocarditis cases. Diagnosis relies on clinical presentation, biomarkers and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) using the modified Lake Louise criteria, with late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) detection sensitivity increasing from 21.6% to 72.0% when imaged after four days of symptoms. Conversely, CAR-T cardiotoxicity is predominantly driven by cytokine release syndrome (CRS), which affects 49-93% of patients with currently licensed products. Severe CRS more than doubles the risk of cardiovascular events, including a 6-10% incidence of LVEF decline and a 4-18% incidence of arrhythmias. Recent advancements include machine learning models to predict MACE and structured screening programs to risk-stratify candidates. Cardiotoxicity remains a significant complication, highlighting the need for vigilant monitoring and early intervention. Management relies on baseline risk assessment and rapid deployment of targeted therapies, such as high-dose methylprednisolone for ICI-myocarditis and IL-6 inhibition (tocilizumab) for CAR-T-related CRS. A multidisciplinary cardio-oncology approach is essential to mitigate risks. With early diagnosis and appropriate immunosuppressive strategies in a multidisciplinary setting, these complications can be better managed, optimising oncological benefits whilst reducing treatment-related morbidity and mortality in majority of patients.
42905164: Prostate cancer remains one of the most common malignancies in men, and its global burden continues to rise. Although androgen deprivation therapy and other standard treatments can provide substantial disease control, advanced tumors may progress to castration-resistant prostate cancer, which is associated with poor outcomes. Preclinical and translational evidence implicates prostate cancer stem-like cells (PCSCs) in treatment persistence, progression, and relapse, without establishing them as the sole cause of resistance in patients. PCSC-associated states share functional traits with normal stem cells, including self-renewal and survival under stress; reduced androgen receptor activity occurs in some, but not all, stem-like populations. Their behavior is influenced by the genomic context, including PTEN loss, TP53/RB1 alterations, SPOP mutations, and TMPRSS2-ERG rearrangements, as well as hypoxia, stromal interactions, and inflammatory signaling. These alterations are not specific markers of PCSC identity. Multiple interconnected pathways, notably PI3K/AKT/mTOR, RAS/MAPK, Hedgehog, Wnt/β-catenin, Hippo, JAK/STAT, Notch, EGFR, and hypoxia-driven HIF signaling, provide candidate therapeutic targets. Additional strategies include modifying the microenvironment to suppress epithelial-to-mesenchymal plasticity, restoring tumor-suppressive microRNAs, and developing checkpoint inhibitors, vaccines, and CAR-T cells against relevant tumor-associated antigens. Most PCSC-specific evidence remains experimental, even when a pathway-directed agent has clinical activity or regulatory approval in a molecularly selected prostate cancer population. Clinical tumor responses do not by themselves demonstrate selective PCSC depletion. This narrative review distinguishes mechanistic findings from clinical outcomes and considers limitations involving marker specificity, model selection, drug delivery, toxicity, and therapeutic escape. Functionally validated biomarkers and appropriately designed combination trials are needed to determine whether targeting PCSC-associated states can improve durable disease control.
42904142: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed outcomes in selected hematologic malignancies, yet its delivery remains constrained by variable efficacy, acute and prolonged toxicities, and complex manufacturing logistics. Artificial intelligence (AI) is being applied across the CAR-T continuum at three distinct levels of evidentiary maturity. Externally validated parsimonious models built on routine clinical and laboratory data including CAR-HEMATOTOX, endothelial activation and stress index (EASIX) and m-EASIX, MyCARe, and gradient-boosting cytokine release syndrome predictors provide deployable risk stratification today. Methodologically sophisticated tools using deep-learning positron emission tomography (PET) segmentation, attention-based digital-pathology analysis, and multimodal fusion of imaging with laboratory and circulating tumor DNA features have demonstrated technical promise but generally lack the multi-center external validation required for clinical-grade deployment. Forward-looking applications, including digital-twin frameworks, large language models, and closed-loop adaptive therapy, remain at the prototype stage and have not yet been validated for CAR-T. This review synthesizes these three tiers, summarizes 18 published AI and statistical-modeling tools in a comparative performance table, and compares data characteristics and AI modeling paradigms across large B cell lymphoma, B cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia, and multiple myeloma. We also identify the implementation realities-absent regulatory clearance, demographic and racial bias in training data, and post-deployment model drift-that condition the field's evolution. The contribution of AI to CAR-T therapy, as the evidence currently stands, is the calibrated quantification of established risk factors rather than the discovery of novel biology, but the methodological and data infrastructure foundations are now in place for the broader transformation that the next decade may enable.
42903357: Follicular lymphoma (FL) is the second most common lymphoma subtype in Europe, with a median age at diagnosis of 60-65 years. It is generally considered an indolent disease, and the median overall survival at diagnosis now likely exceeds 20 years. However, considerable heterogeneity exists. Diagnosis requires adequate biopsy material and a specialized hematopathologist. Staging and prognosis rely on positron emission tomography (PET)-computed tomography (CT). Prognostication at diagnosis is based on several validated clinical prognostic scores. Localized disease is usually treated with radiotherapy ± Rituximab. The treatment of disseminated disease includes active surveillance (or in selected cases Rituximab monotherapy) for low-tumor burden patients, and most often immunochemotherapy (or in selected cases chemo-free therapeutic options), ±antibody maintenance in high-tumor burden patients. For relapsed or refractory disease, treatment with Rituximab-Lenalidomide combination ± Tafasitamab or Epcoritamab from the first relapse and single-agent bispecific antibodies, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapy (CAR-T) cells, and Zanubrutinib-Obinutuzumab after second relapse should be prioritized over immunochemotherapy. Given the long natural history and risk of relapse, careful follow-up is an important part of patient management. Patients should be actively involved in decision-making. In this guideline, we present current evidence-based recommendations for diagnosis, staging, treatment, and follow-up.
42903281: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has achieved remarkable remission rates exceeding 80% in relapsed/refractory pediatric B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (B-ALL), yet 40-50% of patients eventually relapse within the first year. This therapeutic ceiling is not a single failure mode but the convergence of at least four interrelated layers: loss of CAR-T persistence, antigen escape driven by CD19 splicing variants and lineage switch, CAR-T cell-intrinsic exhaustion from chronic tonic signaling, and an immunosuppressive bone marrow microenvironment that actively extinguishes effector function. Our systematic analysis of 226 pediatric-eligible CAR-T trials shows that 95.6% are Phase I-II, 3.5% (8/226) are registered as Phase III/IV, and 58 of 102 completed trials (56.9%) had no outcome recorded in the source database. In this Perspective, we synthesize the molecular mechanisms of CAR-T resistance, contextualize them within the current clinical trial landscape, and critically evaluate emerging engineering strategies-from dual-targeting and armored CAR architectures to CRISPR-edited allogeneic products and in vivo mRNA delivery. We argue that progress depends on both smarter receptor design and structural reforms in trial design, outcome transparency and global collaboration.
42903186: B7-H3 (CD276) is broadly overexpressed across solid tumors and plays active roles in immune evasion, tumor angiogenesis, and metabolic reprogramming. As B7-H3-directed antibody-drug conjugates chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies, and radioimmunotherapy agents advance through clinical trials, non-invasive whole-body imaging of B7-H3 expression has become a pressing clinical need. Tissue biopsy with IHC cannot capture systemic target heterogeneity, and the recent IDeate-PanTumor01 trial found no correlation between baseline B7-H3 H-score and response to ifinatamab deruxtecan-illustrating the gap that molecular imaging must fill. This mini review surveys B7-H3-targeted imaging agents by scaffold class-antibodies, affibodies, nanobodies, and bicyclic peptides-and examines radioimmunotherapy platforms that couple PET-based dosimetry with targeted radionuclide delivery.
42902584: INTRODUCTION: Calreticulin (CALR) plays important roles in protein homeostasis, immune responses, and cell signaling. Mutations in the CALR gene drive BCR:ABL1-negative classical myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) through constitutive activation of the thrombopoietin receptor and generate a tumor-specific neoepitopes, providing a rationale for selective immunotherapy. AREAS COVERED: This review summarizes the biological functions of wild-type calreticulin and the molecular consequences of mutant calreticulin, including loss of endoplasmic reticulum retention, altered subcellular localization, receptor activation, and immunogenic properties. It examines preclinical and clinical evidence for therapeutic strategies targeting mutant calreticulin, including peptide-based vaccines, monoclonal antibodies, T-cell engagers, and chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies. Particular attention is given to INCA033989, a mutant calreticulin-targeting monoclonal antibody currently undergoing clinical evaluation, and emerging evidence of its potential to reduce the mutant cell population while preserving normal hematopoiesis. EXPERT OPINION: Mutant calreticulin represents a promising target for clone-directed therapy, potentially shifting MPN treatment from symptom control toward disease modification. However, the durability and clinical significance of molecular responses remain uncertain. Immune evasion, differences between mutation subtypes, and the need to demonstrate long-term clinical benefit remain important challenges. Combining calreticulin-targeted therapies with approaches addressing oncogenic signaling and inflammation may improve treatment durability and help prevent disease progression.
42901918: Ciltacabtagene autoleucel (cilta-cel) and idecabtagene vicleucel (ide-cel) are approved BCMA-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells approved for the treatment of multiple myeloma. Although the higher efficacy of cilta-cel compared to ide-cel may be related to its unique nanobody binding domain, the constructs also differ in their use of EF1α and MND promoters, respectively, to drive CAR expression.
