To elucidate the basis of cilta-cel's efficacy, we analyzed CAR T cells from 87 patients with multiple myeloma (50 cilta-cel, 37 ide-cel) using flow cytometry and single-cell multi-omics. Cilta-cel showed a 10- fold higher peak expansion and greater persistence, driven by an inflammatory GZMK⁺ T cell subset marked by EOMES expression and motif accessibility, but not exhaustion profile. In myeloma xenograft models, the EF1α promoter in cilta-cel, rather than binding domain, recapitulated increased tumor control, enhanced expansion, and GZMK transcriptional profile compared with the MND promoter (ide-cel). These findings suggest that the efficacy of cilta-cel is linked to an EF1α-driven GZMK⁺ transcriptional trajectory that supports both persistence and effector function.
42901433: Macrophages possess intrinsic tumor-homing and tissue-infiltrating abilities, performing various effector functions, including phagocytosis and antigen presentation. These properties make chimeric antigen receptor macrophages (CAR-M) a promising approach to overcoming major barriers in cellular therapy for solid tumors. This review systematically compares and critically evaluates key design variables that determine the therapeutic activity and clinical feasibility of CAR-M, including CAR architecture, macrophage source, gene-delivery method, and manufacturing strategy. We also discuss emerging engineering approaches tailored to macrophage biology, including macrophage-adapted intracellular signaling, regulation of phagocytic checkpoints, metabolic and phenotypic reprogramming, and combinations with immunomodulatory therapies. Their therapeutic potential and translational boundaries are assessed based on current preclinical evidence and early clinical findings. Notably, the major barriers to clinical translation are shifting from focusing solely on antitumor potency to addressing system-level challenges involving cell source and product consistency, in vivo expansion and persistence, phenotypic stability, off-target toxicity, and scalable manufacturing. Therefore, we propose that next-generation CAR-M development should move beyond conventional optimization of the CAR construct to multidimensional engineering centered on macrophage biology. Coordinated optimization of receptor signaling, antigen recognition, cell-state control, delivery, and safety mechanisms will be essential to balance efficacy, persistence, safety, and manufacturability. This review provides an integrated framework for the rational design and clinical evaluation of CAR-M and the development of next-generation CAR-M cellular therapy platforms.
42901256: Persistent autoantibody production after conventional immunosuppression or B-cell depletion has focused attention on antibody-secreting cells that survive without ongoing proliferation. Long-lived plasma cells (LLPCs) are indispensable for durable protective immunity, but autoreactive members of this compartment may also maintain pathogenic antibodies in selected autoimmune diseases. Interpretation is complicated because longevity is usually inferred from population kinetics, anatomical persistence, transcriptional state, or treatment resistance rather than demonstrated by lineage tracing in humans; neither CD19 loss nor any single surface phenotype is a definitive identifier. We conducted a structured narrative review focused on rheumatic diseases and selected antibody-mediated disorders. We integrate developmental routes, CXCR4-dependent homing, adhesion, BAFF/APRIL receptor biology, stromal contact, proteostatic and metabolic adaptation, and single-cell heterogeneity. Systemic lupus erythematosus and lupus nephritis receive dedicated consideration because renal antibody-secreting-cell signatures distinguish active plasmablast-rich inflammation from LLPC-like persistence in refractory disease. Across diseases, the evidence ranges from direct kinetic or tissue studies to indirect serological observations and therapeutic inference. Plasma-cell-directed therapies-including proteasome inhibition, CD38 depletion, BCMA-directed T-cell engagers or cellular therapy, and immune reconstitution-have produced clinically important signals, but most autoimmune data remain uncontrolled, early-phase, or disease-specific. Niche disruption, apoptosis or autophagy inhibition, and antigen-specific deletion remain preclinical or conceptual. A useful translational framework is therefore not that LLPCs are universal master drivers, but that persistent autoreactive plasma cells may constitute one treatment-relevant disease module whose importance should be demonstrated with tissue, clonal, and longitudinal evidence before intervention.
42900516: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy is less effective in solid tumors than in selected hematologic malignancies because vascular, stromal, spatial, and immunosuppressive barriers restrict cell delivery and function. Local hydrogels and related biomaterials can convert a transient administration into a spatially organized depot, but their benefit depends on more than polymer identity. This review therefore combines a scenario-driven framework-depot versus bolus, intratumoral versus peritumoral placement, unresected versus postsurgical disease, and cell-loaded versus cell-free support-with a materials-centered analysis of formation, administration, time-dependent mechanics, architecture, degradation, biochemical presentation, and manufacturing. Direct evidence is distinguished from adjacent mechanistic evidence and design hypotheses. Across the available studies, the best-supported functions are improved delivered-cell recovery, regional persistence, controlled presentation of supportive cues, and enhanced antitumor activity in selected preclinical models. By contrast, universal material-property optima, clinically validated hydrogel-CAR-T products, and cryopreservation of a final cell-loaded depot have not been established. We define practical tests for gelation and device compatibility, productive egression, material-to-cell fitness, component attribution, and integrated-product safety. A materials-focused comparative table and a 30-study evidence map separate measured values from inferred mechanisms and identify where CAR-T cells were directly loaded, administered separately, manufactured in a matrix, or generated in situ. The resulting framework emphasizes that successful platforms must coordinate material behavior, CAR-T quality, anatomical placement, and clinical workflow rather than maximizing retention or chemical complexity alone.
42898911: Ex vivo expansion is a fundamental yet challenging step in the manufacturing of adoptive cell therapies (ACT), as therapeutic success relies on generating enough functional immune cells while maintaining their phenotype, metabolic fitness, and persistence. This review provides a comprehensive overview of immunomodulatory strategies designed to enhance cell yield during ex vivo expansion, categorizing them into cell-intrinsic and cell-extrinsic approaches. Cell-intrinsic strategies, including gene editing and gene transfer technologies, enable precise modulation of survival pathways, proliferation, metabolic state, and resistance to exhaustion. These tools support the production of more potent and durable immune cell products. In contrast, cell-extrinsic strategies shape immune cell behavior through cytokine supplementation, checkpoint blockade, nutrient and metabolic modulation, feeder cell systems, synthetic activation platforms, and biophysical cues such as oxygen tension and bioreactor-controlled environments. Together, these strategies provide coordinated signals that direct activation, differentiation, and persistence during expansion in culture. The review also highlights key regulatory considerations, including distinctions between genetically and non-genetically modified products, risk assessments associated with human and animal-derived materials, ancillary material qualification, and process scalability for clinical translation. By integrating biological, engineering, and regulatory perspectives, this paper outlines principles for scalable immunomodulation platforms designed with regulatory considerations in mind to advance next-generation ACT manufacturing.
42898905: Cancer immunotherapy has demonstrated remarkable efficacy across multiple tumor types. Despite their significant clinical benefits, most patients with solid tumors remain refractory to immunotherapy, and initial responders frequently develop acquired resistance. Tumor plasticity is a key driver of resistance to cancer immunotherapy. In this review, we discuss how epigenetic and metabolic plasticity of tumor contributes to immunotherapy resistance and highlight emerging strategies targeting these programs to overcome resistance and improve clinical outcomes.
42898659: Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has transformed hematologic oncology, but its application in orthopaedic diseases remains at an early stage. In bone malignancies, including osteosarcoma, chondrosarcoma, Ewing sarcoma, and bone metastases, antigen heterogeneity, limited trafficking and persistence, and the immunosuppressive skeletal microenvironment restrict efficacy. CAR-engineered approaches are also emerging in non-malignant disorders: CD19-directed CAR-T therapy has shown early clinical activity in refractory rheumatoid arthritis and other autoimmune rheumatic diseases, whereas senolytic CAR-T strategies for osteoarthritis remain preclinical. This review summarizes current evidence across malignant and non-malignant orthopaedic conditions, with emphasis on target selection, safety, and translational feasibility. Key barriers include antigen escape, impaired infiltration, limited persistence, local immunosuppression, manufacturing complexity, and on-target/off-tumour toxicity. Emerging strategies include multi-target receptors, chemokine receptor engineering, locoregional delivery, safety-control systems, and allogeneic or point-of-care manufacturing. Current evidence supports CAR-T and related CAR-engineered cells as potential complementary approaches for selected refractory orthopaedic conditions, although further translation requires stronger clinical evidence and improved biological and manufacturing strategies. The Translational Potential of this Article: This review identifies disease-specific targets, barriers, and engineering priorities relevant to translating CAR-engineered cell therapies into orthopaedic practice. These considerations may inform preclinical validation and early-phase trials in refractory bone malignancies and selected non-malignant musculoskeletal disorders.
42898640: In June 2026, satri-cel/CT041, a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell product targeting Claudin18.2, received approval from China's National Medical Products Administration for the treatment of Claudin18.2-positive, HER2-negative advanced gastric/gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma after failure of at least two prior lines of therapy. This marks the first CAR-T product approved worldwide for solid tumours. The approval ends the long-standing debate over whether CAR-T cells can be effective against solid malignancies, yet it simultaneously raises a more pointed issue: in its pivotal randomised controlled trial, median progression-free survival was 3.25 months (95% CI 2.86-4.53) with satri-cel against 1.77 months (95% CI 1.61-2.04) with treatment of physician's choice, giving a hazard ratio of 0.37 (95% CI 0.24-0.56). The two medians differ by 1.48 months; that figure marks where each survival distribution is cut in half and is not the benefit any individual patient can expect, and approval does not equate to a cure. Taking this as a starting point, this review systematically dissects the immunological bottlenecks that constrain CAR-T efficacy in gastrointestinal tumours. We first trace the evidence chain from phase I studies through the randomised controlled trial to exploratory adjuvant-therapy settings and then integrate the landscape of targets-Claudin18.2, glypican-3, carcinoembryonic antigen, mesothelin, and CDH17-within a target-tumour matrix encompassing gastric cancer, colorectal cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, and pancreatic cancer. The core section focuses on four intertwined immunological constraints: spatiotemporal heterogeneity and escape at the antigen level; a therapeutic window shaped jointly by epitope masking within tight junctions and immune privilege of the gastric mucosal stem cell niche-this mechanism not only explains why Claudin18.2-directed CAR-T cells exhibit an acceptable safety profile despite target expression on normal tissues but also provides a paradigm for rational selection of next-generation targets; a suppressive microenvironment composed of regulatory T cells, myeloid-derived suppressor cells, tumour-associated macrophages, transforming growth factor-β, adenosine, and a hypoxic and acidotic metabolic milieu; and CAR-T exhaustion driven by chronic antigen stimulation. We particularly emphasise that metabolic stress and exhaustion are not two parallel obstacles. We put forward a mechanistic model in which persistent antigen stimulation combined with intratumoral hypoxia acts as a "double hit": through mitochondrial dysfunction and reactive oxygen species accumulation, the two inputs raise nuclear factor of activated T-cell (NFAT) activity and so drive the TOX/NR4A-dominated exhaustion program. This model is assembled from chronic-infection and mouse tumour systems and has not been tested in human CAR-T cells or in satri-cel-treated patients. We advance it as a framework for organising the four bottlenecks and for explaining why single-point interventions struggle to lift the efficacy ceiling, not as a demonstrated account. On this basis, we discuss strategies such as armouring, logic gating, transcription factor engineering, gene editing, and chemokine receptor modification, along with combination regimens involving checkpoint inhibition, oncolytic viruses, locoregional administration, and microbiome modulation, and we evaluate alternative platforms including CAR-macrophages, CAR-NK cells, and in vivo CAR-T generation. The watershed has been crossed, but the work of turning 3 months into 30 has only just begun.
42898508: Meningioma is the most common primary intracranial tumor, yet recurrent and high-grade disease has few durable systemic options, and, unlike hematological malignancies, no systematically filtered cell-surface antigen resource exists to guide chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T development. We address this gap not by nominating a trial-ready target but by building two reusable resources: an integrative meningioma surfaceome atlas and a transferable, gate-based framework that separates transcriptomic discovery from CAR-T target nomination. Analyzing single-cell RNA sequencing from eight meningioma patients (GSE183655; 80,220 quality-controlled cells), patient-aware differential expression followed by a curated surfaceome filter (UniProt plasma-membrane localization; extracellular domain ≥20 aa; exclusion of ribosomal, nuclear, cytoplasmic, and secreted proteins) reduced 83 scored candidates to 13 bona fide plasma-membrane (Tier A) antigens, removing prominent false positives such as the nuclear proteins FOXC1 and MGMT, the cytoplasmic enzyme lactate dehydrogenase A (LDHA), and the secreted protein PTGDS. Because expression ranking establishes discovery but not CAR-T suitability, we then applied explicit nomination gates: a systemic-safety score integrating whole-body GTEx transcriptomics with Human Protein Atlas protein-level evidence; a membrane-topology tractability gate distinguishing antibody-accessible single-pass and GPI-anchored ectodomains from multi-pass transporters and tail-anchored proteins; and a safety × coverage metric. Under stringent thresholds (combined safety ≥0.55, tumor-cell detection fraction ≥50%, safety × coverage ≥0.30), no Tier A antigen qualified. Ubiquitously expressed antigens were correctly demoted, including the tetraspanin CD9 (53.2% tumor-cell coverage but pan-tissue protein expression and high plasma abundance), and the highest-ranked transporter SLC7A2 was demoted by multi-pass topology (largest extracellular loop 38 aa) despite favorable transcriptomic safety. Leukemia inhibitory factor receptor (LIFR), a single-pass type I receptor with a contiguous 789-aa ectodomain, was the only antibody-tractable nominee for experimental follow-up yet remained liability laden (combined safety 0.41; safety × coverage 0.135) and is not a validated target. Cross-dataset expression overlap (93.3%) reflected mRNA reproducibility, not CAR-T validity or clinical validation, and generic-antibody docking was exploratory only. All findings are transcriptomic and require surface-level confirmation. This work contributes a reproducible meningioma surfaceome atlas and a transferable nomination framework and shows that rigorous gating leaves no single antigen with a favorable safety × coverage × tractability profile, motivating bispecific and logic-gated CAR-T strategies.
42898331: Radiotherapy is increasingly combined with CAR T cell therapy in B cell lymphomas, but treatment outcome may depend on the irradiation modality. We evaluated minibeam radiation therapy (MBRT) as a partner for CD19 CAR T cells in an orthotopic primary central nervous system (CNS) lymphoma model in immunodeficient rats. CAR T therapy prolonged survival compared with untreated controls. MBRT at 30 Gy followed by CAR T cells five days later produced the longest median survival among radiotherapy-containing regimens and improved outcome compared with conventional radiotherapy (CRT) based combinations. Histopathological findings were consistent with these survival differences. However, MBRT plus CAR T therapy did not significantly outperform CAR T monotherapy. These results indicate that MBRT provides a favorable, non-antagonistic radiotherapy context for CAR T therapy and suggest that radiation modality should be considered when designing combinations of radiotherapy with adoptive cellular therapies.
42898134: Large insert gene editing in ex vivo, primary human T cells represents an important approach for engineering next-generation cellular immunotherapies. While CRISPR-based editing is well-established for small genetic modifications, large insert knock-in remains a technical bottleneck. This review examines current strategies for achieving efficient, precise and safe integration of large genetic elements. We compare delivery methods for CRISPR components, highlighting electroporation of Cas9 ribonucleoproteins as the most efficient but often cytotoxic approach; emerging alternatives such as cell-penetrating peptides and lipid nanoparticles offer improved cell viability at the expense of editing efficiency. The influence of genomic locus selection, guide RNA design and chromatin context on editing outcomes, as well as the role of homology-directed repair (HDR) template design is evaluated. Various template formats-including linear double- and single-stranded DNA, plasmids, circular single-stranded (css) DNA and recombinant adeno-associated virus (rAAV)-are assessed for their efficiency, toxicity and risk of off-target integration. Where possible, cross-study normalisation is used to enable meaningful comparisons. rAAV templates consistently achieve the highest insertion rates but come with concerns regarding cost, size limitations and insertional mutagenesis, whereas non-viral approaches such as cssDNA templates show promise. Additionally, we review the use of small-molecule modulators to enhance HDR efficiency, noting trade-offs between improved insertion rates and potential genomic instability. Overall, successful large insert editing requires balancing of editing efficiency, cell viability and genomic safety considerations. Continued optimisation of delivery systems, template design and repair pathway modulation will be critical for advancing scalable and clinically viable T-cell therapies.
42897856: Gene therapy offers a fundamental approach to treating genetic disorders, malignant tumors, and refractory chronic diseases by directly modifying or replacing defective genes at the molecular level. Driven by policy support, increased investment, and technological innovation, China has achieved remarkable progress in adenoviral and adeno-associated virus (AAV) vectors, gene editing, genetically engineered immune cells, oncolytic microorganisms, and small nucleic acid drugs. This review provides a comprehensive narrative overview of the technical principles, product pipelines, and clinical advances in these fields. Notable achievements include the approval of AAV-based gene therapy products in China, the entry of multiple in vivo and ex vivo gene editing therapies into clinical trials, a leading number of CAR-T trials worldwide with expansion into solid tumors and autoimmune diseases, encouraging efficacy of oncolytic virotherapy in liver cancer and melanoma, and positive clinical data of small interfering RNA/antisense oligonucleotide drugs for chronic hepatitis B and hypercholesterolemia. However, challenges remain including suboptimal tissue specificity, off-target risks, limited cargo capacity, high production costs, and poor accessibility. Future directions should focus on tissue-selective vectors, precise editing tools, off-the-shelf cell products, scalable manufacturing, and improved regulatory frameworks. With abundant clinical resources and strong manufacturing capabilities, China is poised to play a significant role in the global gene therapy landscape.
42897095: BACKGROUND: Relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (R/R B-ALL) patients exhibit heterogeneous responses to CD19 chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. However, current studies primarily focus on the CAR-T cells or the leukemia blasts, and the patient's intrinsic molecular characteristics before treatment remain poorly understood. METHODS: Fifteen R/R B-ALL patients enrolled in a phase II, single-arm clinical trial (NCT04684147) were stratified at a three-month landmark into 8 good responders and 7 poor responders. Clinical characteristics, genetic alterations and pre-treatment bone marrow transcriptomics were compared between groups, and an exploratory gene-expression score was derived. RESULTS: Differential expression and enrichment analyses identified a myeloid-like signature and upregulation of myeloid-related genes in poor responders. Seven myeloid-related genes were examined in independent patient cohorts, in B-ALL cell lines and at single-cell resolution in one patient; three were expressed by the leukemic cells themselves and four predominantly by monocytes and macrophages. A separate, variance-derived seven-gene least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) score separated response groups in the discovery cohort (apparent area under the curve, AUC 1.00), with bias-corrected and external estimates of approximately 0.57-0.59 (external cohort AUC 0.592, 95% confidence interval 0.356-0.828). CONCLUSIONS: Pre-treatment transcriptomic profiling revealed a myeloid-like signature in R/R B-ALL patients with poor CD19 CAR-T response, warranting further investigation as a candidate correlate of treatment outcome.
42896626: BACKGROUND: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) commonly affects older patients > 65 years old, with chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy becoming an increasingly valuable treatment modality for relapsed/refractory (R/R) disease. Real world data on safety, efficacy, and management practices of CAR-T for older patients are important to inform clinical practice and referral. OBJECTIVE: To compare efficacy and toxicities of axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) and tisagenlecleucel (tisa-cel) in younger (age <65) and older (age ≥ 65) patients with R/R DLBCL, and to describe clinical management practices for delivery of care to older patients. STUDY DESIGN: We conducted a retrospective, multicenter analysis of 351 adult patients with R/R DLBCL using data from the Cell Therapy Consortium registry. Patients who underwent apheresis for commercial axi-cel or tisa-cel products from early 2018 to late 2021 were compared by age: 194 patients < 65 years old and 157 patients ≥ 65 years old. Survival was estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method with 95% confidence intervals and compared using the log-rank test. Univariate and multivariate Cox proportional hazards regression was performed to identify factors associating with progression-free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS). RESULTS: 328 patients (93.5%) were infused with CAR-T product. Combining all CAR-T products, younger and older groups yielded similar overall response rates (ORR, 61% vs 64%) and complete response rates (CR, 43% vs 49%). When evaluating only those who received axi-cel (n = 65), the older group had improved ORR (82% vs 65%, p = 0.02) and CR rates (63% vs 47%, p = 0.04) compared to younger patients. Median PFS (4.4 months in younger vs 6.8 months in older, p=0.44) and OS (22 months in younger vs 18 months in older, p=0.85) were similar between the two groups. In this cohort, 70% developed cytokine release syndrome (CRS, 6% grade > 3) with no significant difference by age overall or within same CAR-T product. In total, 71 patients (38%) developed immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) with 23% being grade ≥ 3. There was no difference in any grade ICANS between younger and older patients. On multivariate analysis, overall mortality was increased in patients with high IPI (HR 1.71, p < 0.01) and bulky disease (HR 1.96, p < 0.01). Age group or CAR-T product were not associated with PFS or OS at 2 years. Rates of early infection, severe (grade >3) cytopenias at 3 months, and 100-day and 1-year non-relapse mortality (NRM) were also similar between younger and older patients. CONCLUSION: Data from our Cell Therapy Consortium retrospective analysis demonstrate that CAR-T recipients older than 65 yrs experience favorable outcomes and manageable toxicity similar to younger patients. Our results support the practice that age alone should not be a barrier to CAR-T consultation or therapy.
42896405: BACKGROUND: Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell (CAR T-cell) therapy is a promising treatment option for patients with refractory or relapsed B-cell malignancies. The success of this therapy depends on the efficient collection of lymphocytes (CD3+ T cells) through apheresis. This study analyzed the factors influencing CD3+ cell counts in apheresis products for CAR T-cell therapy. METHODS: This exploratory analysis evaluated patients enrolled in the registration phase I/II trials of talicabtagene autoleucel at a tertiary care oncology centre in Western India. Patients were enrolled after obtaining informed consent. The study was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee and the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), and registered with the Clinical Trials Registry of India. A total of 48 autologous lymphocytapheresis procedures were performed on 44 patients with refractory or relapsed lymphoma (predominantly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma) or B-acute lymphoblastic leukemia. Pre-apheresis hematological parameters and flow cytometry were used to estimate absolute lymphocyte counts and peripheral blood CD3+ cell counts. Predictive factors for CD3+ cells in the product were analyzed using the Pearson correlation coefficient and regression models by the Statistical Package for Social Sciences software (Version 25.0, Armonk, NY: IBM Corp.), and p-values <0.05 were considered statistically significant. RESULTS: Pre-apheresis parameters like total leukocyte count, absolute lymphocyte count, and circulating CD3⁺ cell count were all positively correlated with the absolute CD3+ cell yield in the apheresis product (p < 0.05). Importantly, these associations remained significant in multivariate analysis, highlighting their independent predictive value for the harvested CD3+ count. Additionally, lower pre-apheresis hematocrit and higher platelet levels were independently associated with reduced CD3+ recovery. Notably, the targeted CD3+ cell dose was successfully achieved in 96 % (46/48) of collections. CONCLUSION: Pre-apheresis total leukocyte count, absolute lymphocyte counts, CD3+ cells, hematocrit, and platelet counts are key factors influencing the successful collection of CD3+ cells during apheresis. Understanding these variables is crucial for optimizing lymphocyte collection for CAR T-cell manufacturing.
42896102: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS) affect most patients receiving axicabtagene ciloleucel (axi-cel) for relapsed or refractory large B-cell lymphoma (LBCL). Based on pre-clinical data, we hypothesized that prophylactic IFN-γ blockade could prevent toxicity without impairing efficacy. We initiated an open-label phase 2 trial (NCT06550141) evaluating single-dose emapalumab one day before axi-cel. Here, we report the first two patients to caution against the pre-emptive emapalumab use prior axi-cel: Both developed treatment-refractory toxicities including high-grade ICANS and overlapping CRS-IEC-HS requiring multiple immunomodulatory agents. CAR T-cell expansion exceeded levels reported in ZUMA-1 and a standard-of-care axi-cel cohort at our institution. Despite therapeutic emapalumab and suppressed free IFN-γ, IL-2 and sIL-2R were markedly elevated, suggesting CRS was driven independent of IFN-γ. Both patients achieved complete responses, suggesting preserved efficacy. Given the unanticipated severity and refractoriness of toxicities, recruitment with this design was discontinued and the protocol was amended.
42895279: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: To summarize recent advances in systemic sclerosis (SSc) highlighted at the 2026 World Scleroderma Congress, focusing on early disease, immunovascular mechanisms, and emerging therapeutic strategies. RECENT FINDINGS: Recent data support a paradigm shift in SSc, demonstrating that disease onset occurs during a very early phase (VEDOSS) characterized by early immune activation and microvascular dysfunction. Type I interferon-driven pathways are increasingly implicated in vascular and myocardial involvement, reinforcing the concept of a shared immunovascular axis across organ systems. Advances in multimodal imaging and circulating biomarkers enable detection of subclinical organ disease, while multi-omic and data-driven approaches are redefining disease subsets beyond traditional classifications. In parallel, novel therapeutic strategies - including targeted immune modulation, autologous haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (AHSCT), and emerging CAR-T approaches - are driving a transition toward earlier, mechanism-based intervention. SUMMARY: Systemic sclerosis is increasingly understood as a dynamic continuum of autoimmune/inflammatory and fibrotic mechanisms that can be identified through imaging, biohumoral, and functional insights, thus enabling a very early/early diagnosis, a risk stratification, and a precision-based therapeutic approach.
42894313: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has shown limited efficacy in glioblastoma (GB), largely because of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). We have previously demonstrated that the ligand-based mCD70-directed construct mCAR27 specifically eliminates CD70⁺ GB cells in vitro, and induces durable tumor remission with prolonged survival in a syngeneic model of orthotopic GB. Despite the therapeutic promise of CD70 as a GB CAR-T cell target, the impact of CD70-directed CAR-T cells on the brain tumor immune landscape after target interception remains unexplored. Here, we independently confirmed a tumorigenic role for CD70 in murine GB by performing bulk RNA sequencing and in vivo experiments. Next, we applied single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq) to decipher the transcriptome of GB-infiltrating immune cells in immunocompetent mice bearing CD70+ GB after intratumoral mCAR27 therapy. CAR-T cell treatment expanded adoptively transferred cells and was associated with increased endogenous Cd8⁺ T-cell infiltration, alongside a reduction in immunosuppressive populations, including Tregs and anti-inflammatory M2-like macrophages, but also subsets of dendritic and natural-killer cells. CD70 expression was detected on multiple GB-infiltrating immune subsets, notably Tregs and M2-like macrophages. Transcriptionally, mCAR27-mediated GB remission led to a coordinated downregulation of type-I interferon-stimulated genes and immunosuppressive mediators such as Arg1, Tgfbi, Cd274, Pdcd1lg2 and Lag3, coupled with upregulation of genes involved in inflammatory resolution, findings consistent with attenuation of GB-derived inflammatory stress and immunosuppression. Collectively, we showcase that CD70-directed CAR-T cell therapy remodels the post-treatment immune landscape towards resolution of inflammation and reduced immunosuppression, supporting sustained immune surveillance.
42894261: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy has transformed the treatment of hematologic malignancies and established a new paradigm for engineered cellular immunotherapy. However, its broader clinical application remains constrained by complex autologous manufacturing, high cost, limited scalability, variable product quality, suboptimal efficacy in solid tumors, and treatment-related toxicities. To address these challenges, recent advances in CAR-T cell therapy can be viewed across four interconnected dimensions: functional engineering, manufacturing innovation, alternative cell sources, and in vivo CAR programming. Functional engineering includes cytokine-armored, checkpoint-resistant, multi-targeting, and modular or switchable CAR platforms designed to enhance efficacy, persistence, and safety. In parallel, manufacturing innovations such as shortened culture protocols, automated closed systems, and preservation of less differentiated T-cell states aim to improve product potency while reducing production time and complexity. Alternative cell sources, including allogeneic donor-derived and induced pluripotent stem cell (iPSC)-derived platforms, may further enable standardized, scalable, and potentially off-the-shelf therapies. Finally, in vivo CAR programming has emerged as a fourth dimension in which endogenous immune cells are directly engineered within patients using viral or non-viral gene delivery systems. This review summarizes these interconnected advances and discusses how they may collectively shape the next generation of CAR-based immune therapies.
42893828: Relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) remains a challenging condition despite many advances in immunotherapies. Outcomes are particularly dismal in patients who are refractory to these three major classes of proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, monoclonal antibodies (mAbs), and chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies. Novel bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) have shown some promising efficacy in heavily pretreated patients, even those with triple- and penta-refractory disease. Talquetamab is a BsAb recently approved for the treatment of relapsed and refractory multiple myeloma. Talquetamab demonstrated a high overall response rate of approximately 70%, including in patients that are previously treated with T-cell therapies. The safety profile of talquetamab is consistent with other BsAbs, with similar adverse events. The efficacy of talquetamab and other therapies, including CAR-T cell treatments, remains an area of active research, as resistance to anti-B-cell maturation antigen therapies poses a clinical challenge. Current trials are exploring the use of talquetamab in combination therapies. There is now adequate data to further support talquetamab's efficacy, making it a very important addition to the RRMM treatment domain.
42891071: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy provides substantial clinical benefits in hematologic malignancies. However, cell engineering using conventional viral vectors is costly, labor intensive, and prone to safety risks, while electroporation-induced cellular damage limits manufacturing scalability. This study reports a safe, high-efficiency, nonviral platform for generating mRNA-engineered CAR T cells. Herein, eight ionizable lipids are synthesized and formulated into lipid nanoparticles. Systematic screening and structural optimization identified lipid 6 as the lead candidate. Transfection efficiency is validated by delivering enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) mRNA into DC2.4, peripheral blood mononuclear, dendritic, and natural killer cells. Murine models confirm robust in vivo expression and a favorable safety profile. Lipid 6-mediated delivery of MUC1 mRNA generates MUC1-CAR T cells characterized by high surface receptor expression and potent cytotoxicity against MUC1-positive tumor cells. These findings establish lipid 6 as a feasible strategy for primary human T cell engineering, facilitating functional CAR expression with minimal toxicity.
42890994: Autoimmune diseases are chronic immune-mediated disorders that, in their systemic forms, such as systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), systemic sclerosis (SSc), idiopathic inflammatory myopathies, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody (ANCA)-associated vasculitis (AAV), remain associated with progressive organ damage, impaired quality of life, and excess mortality despite conventional immunosuppression. A substantial proportion of patients experience refractory disease, recurrent flares, and glucocorticoid dependence, underscoring the need for therapies that address the underlying disease process rather than merely suppressing symptoms. Chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy, originally developed for B-cell malignancies, has emerged as a potential paradigm shift by achieving deep, tissue-level B-cell depletion followed by immune reconstitution, a process often described as an "immune reset." This narrative review summarizes the immunological rationale, clinical evidence, safety profile, and future directions of B-cell-directed (anti-CD19) CAR-T therapy in autoimmune disease. Current evidence identifies refractory SLE as the most mature indication, with reproducible drug-free remission, seroconversion, and durable responses across independent cohorts. Early studies in inflammatory myopathies and SSc report encouraging responses and reduced immunosuppressive requirements, whereas evidence in AAV remains preclinical. Toxicities such as cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity appear less frequent and less severe than in oncology, although infections and hypogammaglobulinemia require monitoring. High cost, complex manufacturing, and limited long-term data remain major barriers, while allogeneic CAR-natural killer cells and in vivo engineering may improve scalability. Larger controlled studies with longer follow-up are needed before routine clinical use.
42890256: INTRODUCTION: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of B-cell malignancies. However, strategies that improve the modularity and controllability of CAR signaling could broaden its applicability and safety across additional clinical contexts. Here, we describe a regulable CAR T-cell platform based on split intein-mediated protein trans-splicing (PTS) to conditionally reconstitute functional receptors in primary T-cells. METHODS: As a proof of concept, we engineered a split CAR targeting CD1a (NCT05679895), a surface antigen expressed in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). The system consists of a membrane-anchored C-terminal scaffold containing the IMPDH.1C split intein fused to 4-1BB and CD3ζ signaling domains, and a soluble N-terminal adaptor composed of an anti-CD1a single-chain variable fragment (scFv) fused to the complementary IMPDH.1N split intein. RESULTS: Upon delivery of the adaptor module, the intein fragments undergo PTS, generating a functional membrane-bound CD1a CAR with splicing efficiencies of 85%. Reconstituted CAR T-cells exhibited antigen-specific cytotoxicity against CD1a+ T-ALL cells coupled to high levels of interferon-γ secretion. DISCUSSION: These findings demonstrate that split intein-mediated CAR reconstitution enables a modular platform for conditional CAR reconstitution and transient control of receptor availability.
42890243: INTRODUCTION: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy is a standard treatment for several hematological malignancies, yet patient-specific responses and toxicities remain hard to predict. Although multiple covariates and risk scores exist, their prognostic accuracy remains limited. METHODS: We prospectively measured CAR T-cell kinetics in peripheral blood of 92 patients with B-cell malignancies using multicolor flow cytometry. To explore underlying mechanisms, we developed a mechanistic model of CAR T-cell and tumor cell interactions. RESULTS: We captured four phases of CAR T-cell kinetics in peripheral blood: distribution, expansion, contraction, and persistence. Patients with weak expansion or deep contraction are more likely to relapse. When fitted to the 46 patients with suDicient data points, the model reproduces individual CAR T-cell kinetics but fails to predict outcomes using uniform tumor parameters. We demonstrate that identical CAR T-cell dynamics may result from diDerent tumor features, including growth rate, initial burden, or antigen density. Accurately estimating these tumor-specific factors may improve relapse prediction, while common surrogates like blood lactate dehydrogenase, International Prognostic Index score, or Ann-Arbor stage do not. CONCLUSION: We conclude that CAR T-cell kinetics within the first month can serve as early prognostic markers. Integrating tumor burden estimates is required to reconcile kinetics with individual outcomes and may, upon prospective validation, further improve risk stratification in patients with B-cell malignancies receiving CAR T-cell therapy.
42890208: Retinoblastoma (RB) is an aggressive pediatric intraocular malignancy in which chemoresistant or relapsed disease often requires enucleation, leading to vision loss. GD2-targeted chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells are promising for GD2-positive tumors, but PD-L1-mediated immunosuppression and reduced surface antigen density can limit their activity. We developed a fifth-generation anti-GD2 CAR (GD2-CAR5), defined here as a fourth-generation backbone that additionally drives secretion of an anti-PD-L1 single-chain variable fragment (scFv) from the same transgene cassette, incorporating a humanized 3F8 anti-GD2 scFv and CD28, 4-1BB, CD27, and CD3ζ signaling domains. CAR surface expression and scFv secretion were confirmed in primary transduced T cells, and the secreted scFv bound and blocked PD-L1 on target cells during co-culture. Against both high- and low-antigen-density RB cells, GD2-CAR5 and fourth-generation GD2-CAR4 T cells mediated comparable cytotoxicity and secreted comparable levels of granzyme B and IFN-γ; however, only GD2-CAR5 T cells were cytotoxic at the lowest effector-to-target ratio tested against low-density targets. Under repeated antigen re-stimulation, GD2-CAR5 T cell numbers remained above baseline through day 12, whereas GD2-CAR4 T cell numbers declined, without increased exhaustion marker expression. These findings provide in vitro proof-of-concept and support further preclinical evaluation in relapsed or refractory RB.
42889616: Multiple myeloma (MM) outcomes have improved with proteasome inhibitors, immunomodulatory drugs, anti-CD38 antibodies, and transplantation, yet a subset of patients with high-risk MM (HRMM) continues to relapse early and die prematurely. Immune effector therapies (IET)-B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)- and G protein-coupled receptor class C group 5 member D (GPRC5D)-directed chimeric antigen receptor T cells (CAR-T) and bispecific antibodies-have transformed the treatment of relapsed/refractory MM. However, their benefit in HRMM remains incompletely defined. This review describes how HRMM is defined in the IET-era distinguishing baseline biological/genomic risk, clinical high-risk phenotypes, and IET-specific adverse predictors. The International Myeloma Society/International Myeloma Working Group consensus integrates adverse cytogenetics and beta-2 microglobulin, whereas functional high-risk disease, extramedullary disease (EMD), plasma cell leukemia (PCL), high tumor burden, inflammation, and prior BCMA exposure identify aggressive disease in relapsed patients. Across pivotal trials, CAR-T therapy, particularly ciltacabtagene autoleucel, and selected bispecific antibodies retain activity in high-risk cytogenetic subgroups, whereas EMD and PCL remain associated with inferior responses and short progression-free survival. Emerging dual-antigen and trispecific engagers, along with novel targets such as FcRH5 and CD70, aim to overcome antigen escape. Prospective, biology-informed studies are needed to achieve durable disease control in HRMM.
42889518: BACKGROUND: Cytokine release syndrome (CRS) is a life-threatening complication of chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy. Macrophages/monocytes are mediators of CRS. Tripterygium glycosides is an immunomodulator, which could inhibit macrophages/monocytes in animal models. METHODS: Two patients with relapsed and refractory hematological malignancies developed CRS after receiving CAR-T therapy. They received short-term Tripterygium glycosides orally. RESULTS: Both patients showed rapid mitigation of fever with evidently decrease in elevated inflammatory cytokines within 72 hours. The patients' monocytes diminished remarkably, while CAR-T cells were negligibly affected. Treatment of 30 ng/ml triptolide in ex vivo cultured patients' blood for 24 hours selectively deplete over half of monocytes. Single-cell RNA sequencing suggested selective depletion of CD14 + CD16+ monocytes with decreased pro-inflammatory cytokines. CONCLUSION: The low-cost and orally available Tripterygium glycosides could be a promising alternative for CAR-T induced CRS, as well as other diseases complicated with CRS, e.g. coronavirus disease 2019.
42889508: T cell receptor (TCR)-like antibodies that recognize a peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) can enable precise targeting of cancer cells, but developing single-domain binders with high specificity and affinity is challenging. Here, we report the computational design and experimental validation of a TCR-like human heavy chain variable (VH) domain antibody that specifically recognizes the Wilms' tumor 1 protein (WT1)-derived peptide RMFPNAPYL presented by HLA-A*02:01/β2-microglobulin (RMF/HLA-A*02). Starting from the crystal structure of a Fab antibody bound to RMF/HLA-A*02, we repurposed the soluble trastuzumab-derived VH scaffold to bind RMF/HLA-A*02. The resulting VH domain, αRMF_VH, spans all 9 peptide residues and showed no binding to a control pMHC with a different peptide. Fusion of 1 or 2 αRMF_VH molecules to human serum albumin domain III yielded monovalent and bivalent constructs with good biophysical properties. The monovalent construct bound selectively to RMF/HLA-A*02 with 81 nM affinity, and when expressed as part of a chimeric antigen receptor on T cells, it functioned as an antigen-recognition domain to selectively activate T cells in the presence of RMF/HLA-A*02-positive cells. The bivalent construct exhibited a dramatically increased apparent binding affinity of 0.37 nM. When both constructs were engineered into the bispecific T cell engager (TCE) format containing an anti-CD3 Fv, the bivalent TCE induced antigen-dependent cytotoxicity much more effectively than the monovalent TCE. These results demonstrate a viable strategy to develop high-specificity, peptide-focused TCR-like VH domain antibodies that can be readily extended into potent bivalent TCEs for pMHC-targeted therapeutics.
42889486: Large B-cell lymphomas, particularly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), provide a clinically important model in which tumor-intrinsic programs, immune recognition, effector-cell fitness, and tissue architecture jointly shape response and resistance to immunotherapy. Although molecular classification has refined the understanding of lymphoma biology, relapse after chemoimmunotherapy, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, CD20×CD3 bispecific antibodies, antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), and immune-combination strategies cannot be explained by genetics or target-antigen expression alone. Single-cell and spatial multi-omics now allow lymphoma to be interpreted as a spatial immune ecosystem composed of malignant B-cell states, exhausted or regulatory T-cell programs, myeloid suppressive hubs, stromal and vascular compartmentalization, metabolic gradients, and local communication networks. This Review synthesizes recent DLBCL and large B-cell lymphoma ecosystem studies from a cancer-immunology perspective, emphasizing how spatial immune organization may influence effector access, antigen engagement, macrophage-mediated suppression, antibody exposure, and treatment-associated spatial change. We propose a treatment-matched validation framework that connects high-dimensional discovery to formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE)-compatible pathology assays, including reduced marker panels for CAR T-cell therapy, bispecific antibodies, ADC-containing therapy, and immune-combination trials. Throughout, we distinguish observed tissue organization from computationally inferred communication and experimentally validated mechanisms. The resulting framework is intended as a trial-design and biomarker-development roadmap, not as a current clinical allocation algorithm.
42889303: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered natural killer (NK) cells represent a promising platform for cancer immunotherapy; however, optimization of CAR architecture and additional engineering strategies remain necessary to improve their functional activity. In this study, we generated CD19/BCMA dual-target CAR constructs based on tandem and bicistronic configurations with or without membrane-bound interleukin-15 (mbIL-15), and further evaluated engineered virus-like particle (eVLP)-mediated CREM editing as an additional strategy for CAR-NK cell engineering. Four CAR configurations were evaluated in primary human T and NK cells for CAR expression, cytotoxicity, cytokine production, and proliferative activity. Bicistronic CD19/BCMA CAR-mbIL-15 cells exhibited enhanced functional activity compared with corresponding tandem CAR-mbIL-15 cells, including increased tumor-cell killing and activation-associated functional responses in vitro. In a CD19/BCMA-positive leukemia xenograft model, bicistronic CD19/BCMA CAR-mbIL-15 T and NK cells reduced tumor burden, delayed disease progression, and prolonged survival. Furthermore, eVLP-mediated CREM editing achieved efficient genome modification in primary NK cells and remained compatible with subsequent CAR engineering. CREM-edited CAR-NK cells exhibited increased cytotoxic activity compared with unedited CAR-NK cells in vitro. Collectively, these findings support the development of modular CAR-NK engineering strategies integrating CAR architecture optimization, membrane-bound cytokine armoring, and transient genome engineering.
42889281: Plasmablastic lymphoma is a rare, aggressive large B cell lymphoma characterized by plasmablastic morphology, terminal B cell (plasma cell) differentiation, frequent loss of conventional B cell markers, and poor clinical outcomes. Although classically associated with immunodeficiency and Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection, plasmablastic lymphoma has also been described as an uncommon mechanism of relapse after CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy. We report a 69-year-old man with a remote history of chronic lymphocytic leukemia/small lymphocytic lymphoma and subsequent refractory diffuse large B cell lymphoma (DLBCL) who developed rapidly progressive, CD19-negative plasmablastic lymphoma approximately 1 month after CD19-directed CAR-T therapy. Although DLBCL was of a nongerminal-center phenotype with expression of pan-B markers including CD19 and lack of CD138, the post-CAR-T transformed lymphoma demonstrated acquisition of plasmablastic morphology and CD138 expression, loss of pan-B markers and negative for EBV by in situ hybridization and HHV8 by immunostaining. Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) on the plasmablastic lymphoma showed a MYC::IGH fusion and low-level MYC copy gain that were absent in the antecedent DLBCL. Disease dissemination was later confirmed on left pleural fluid cytology a few days before the patient passed away. This case highlights EBV and HHV8 negative plasmablastic transformation as a rare but important post-CAR-T relapse pattern and underscores the need for repeat biopsy, comprehensive paired immunophenotyping, and molecular studies in patients with atypical progression after cellular therapy.
42889049: The presence of polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) in the tumor microenvironment is associated with lower survival rates for cancer patients. Presumably due to the immunosuppressive activity of neutrophils (also known as Myeloid-Derived Suppressor Cell (MDSC) activity). We investigated whether this MDSC activity shows any selectivity in suppressing specific lymphocyte subsets. Our data show that CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, both naive and memory fractions, are sensitive to PMN-MDSC activity. Similarly, regulatory T cells, believed to play an important immunosuppressive function themselves, were affected too. In contrast, the more innate-like γδ T cells and Natural Killer (NK) cells were left intact. Our data suggest that Chimeric Antigen Receptor (CAR)-NK and γδ CAR-T cell immunotherapy may be less susceptible to PMN-MDSC activity. Therefore, using such MDSC-resistant innate cells as cellular products may be of advantage over the common αβ CAR-T cell therapies. Additionally, further deciphering the exact mechanisms by which neutrophils suppress αβ T cells could lead to improved T cell immunotherapies.
42888846: Allogeneic CAR-T therapy offers an "off-the-shelf" alternative to autologous CAR-T, but faces graft-versus-host rejection (GVH) and host-versus-graft rejection (HVG). Conventional TCR/MHC elimination compromises persistence and increase NK susceptibility. Here, we developed a next-generation UCAR-T strategy that avoids TCR/MHC disruption while addressing donor-cell alloreactivity and host-mediated rejection. First, we eliminated CD4/CD8 to reduce alloreactivity while preserving TCR integrity and potentially TCR/CD3-mediated fitness, although in vivo xGvHD protection remains to be determined. In parallel, we identified CD70 as a marker selectively upregulated on alloreactive immune cells, enabling targeted removal of HVG-driving subsets. Because CD70 is also induced during T-cell activation and further enhanced following CD4/CD8 knockout, we additionally deleted CD70 to prevent fratricide, generating a CD4/CD8/CD70 triple-negative UCAR-T backbone (eDN70(-) UCAR-T). As proof-of-concept, we incorporated both CD19- and CD70-targeting CARs to generate eDN70(-)19/70CAR-T cells, which showed superior expansion, reduced exhaustion, and greater resistance to HVG pressure. Furthermore, these cells demonstrated durable tumor control and robust recall responses in vivo, with preliminary tissue-level safety from the high-dose study. Collectively, our findings establish eDN70(-) UCAR-T cells as a versatile platform capable of overcoming the persistence limitations of current allogeneic CAR-T therapies, with the CD19/CD70 dual-target configuration serving as a representative implementation of this strategy.
42888448: Over recent years, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy has markedly improved outcomes for patients with relapsed or refractory hematological malignancies. Nevertheless, a substantial proportion of patients still experience relapse or progression after treatment, driven by factors including antigen escape, suboptimal CAR-T cell expansion and persistence, functional exhaustion, and remodeling of the tumor microenvironment. In the context of managing patients who fail initial CAR-T therapy, CAR-T-centered sequential therapy has been increasingly investigated as a potential therapeutic approach. The selection of therapeutic targets and treatment approaches may be informed by resistance mechanisms, changes in target antigen expression, and disease progression patterns following prior treatment, with the aim of prolonging disease control and improving long-term outcomes. This review summarizes recent progress in CAR-T-centered sequential therapy, with particular emphasis on same-target retreatment, switching to different antigens, multi-target stepwise CAR-T regimens, and the sequential integration of CAR-T with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, radiotherapy, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and other immunomodulatory approaches. We further discuss the biological rationale and clinical settings of these CAR-T-centered sequential approaches in the context of antigen escape, CAR-T cell functional decline, tumor clonal evolution, and immune microenvironment remodeling. Additionally, we discuss factors that may inform the selection of subsequent regimens, including the initial treatment response, antigen status at relapse, CAR-T cell persistence, and the patient's therapeutic window, as well as the clinical settings in which these sequential approaches have been explored.
42888436: The rapidly global deployment of COVID-19 mRNA-LNP vaccines established the clinical feasibility of combining RNA medicine with LNP delivery systems, transforming a long-standing experimental concept into a scalable therapeutic modality, previously considered impossible. Currently, the value of mRNA-LNPs has been expanding from infectious disease vaccines to cancer immunotherapy, personalized neoantigen vaccination, in vivo immune-cell engineering, protein replacement therapy, mRNA-encoded biologics and genome editing, with particular relevance to hematology and oncology. However, in hematologic and oncologic settings, therapeutic success is constrained by biological barriers that less prominent in prophylactic vaccination. Systemically administered LNPs are strongly influenced by hepatic sequestration, protein corona formation and mononuclear-phagocyte clearance; solid tumors additionally present heterogeneous vasculature, variable enhanced permeability and retention, dense extracellular matrix, elevated interstitial pressure and limited intratumoral diffusion. Hematologic applications face a different set of constraints, including access to spleen and bone marrow, selective delivery to T cells, NK cells and hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), and preservation of the normal marrow niche. In this Review, we therefore discuss the molecular and principles of formulation that underpin mRNA-LNP performance in hematology and oncology, including mRNA engineering, lipid nanoparticle architecture, intracellular trafficking and selective organ targeting(SORT) delivery strategies, oncology applications spanning neoantigen vaccines, tumor-microenvironment reprogramming, mRNA-encoded biologics, gene editing and combination therapy; and hematology applications including in vivo CAR-T, CAR-NK and HSPC engineering. We further consider how inefficient extrahepatic delivery, limited endosomal escape, context-dependent reactogenicity, repeat-dosing constraints and the manufacturing complexity of individualized products continue to limit broader clinical translation. Emerging strategies, including artificial-intelligence-guided RNA and lipid design, self-amplifying RNA, circular RNA and next-generation thermostable formulations, may help address these application limitations in the fields of hematology and oncology.
